title: A perfume advert
text: The advert shows a young woman in the [[foreground]]. She is wearing a gold dress. The [[lighting]] is soft and warm. The [[colour]] gold [[suggests|suggest]] that she is [[wealthy]].

title: A sports poster
text: The poster shows a footballer. The [[camera angle]] is low, so he looks [[powerful]]. His [[facial expression]] is [[serious]]. The [[slogan]] says “Never stop”.

title: A charity advert
text: The [[image]] shows a small child alone in a dark street. The child looks cold and [[vulnerable]]. The dark [[lighting]] [[creates|create]] a sad mood. The [[purpose]] of the advert is to make people give money.

title: A magazine cover
text: The magazine cover shows a famous singer. Her [[pose]] is [[confident]]: she has her hands on her hips. The [[headline]] is “Queen of Pop”. The [[target audience]] is probably teenage girls.

title: A family advert
text: The advert shows a family in a kitchen. The mother is cooking and the father is reading. This is a [[traditional]] [[representation]] of a family. Some people think it [[reinforces|reinforce]] a [[stereotype]].

title: A news photograph
text: The photo shows a nurse in a hospital. Her [[facial expression]] is kind and [[caring]]. The [[headline]] describes her as a hero. This is a [[positive]] [[representation]] of nurses.

title: A car advert
text: The [[setting]] is a [[modern]] city at night. A man in smart [[clothing]] is driving an expensive car. He looks [[successful]]. The advert [[suggests|suggest]] that the car will make you successful too.

title: A phone advert
text: In the [[background]], there is a busy street. In the [[foreground]], a teenager is smiling at her phone. Her [[body language]] is relaxed and [[friendly]]. The bright colours [[create]] a happy mood.

title: Two sports adverts
text: The first advert shows a [[strong]] man lifting weights. The second advert shows a strong woman running. The second advert [[challenges|challenge]] the [[stereotype]] that women are [[weak]]. The first advert does not.

title: A close-up photo
text: This image is a [[close-up]] of an old man's face. We can see every [[detail]] of his skin. He is not smiling. The close-up helps the [[audience]] to feel sad for him.

title: A film poster
text: The poster shows a superhero in a red [[costume]]. She is standing in front of a burning building. Her [[pose]] shows that she is brave and [[independent]]. The [[language]] on the poster is short and exciting.

title: How to analyse an image
text: When you [[analyse]] an image, look closely at the [[details|detail]]. [[Identify|identify]] the creative choices, such as colour and lighting. Then [[explain]] what each choice suggests. Use [[evidence]] from the image to [[support]] your ideas.

title: Teenagers in the news
text: Many news stories show teenagers in a [[negative]] way. They show young people as lazy or angry. This is not [[realistic]], because most teenagers are [[responsible]]. A better [[representation]] would show [[ordinary]] teenagers at school.

title: A football fan
text: The photo shows a girl at a football match. Her [[clothing]] is the team's colours, red and white. This shows her [[identity]] as a fan. She is part of a [[group]], but she is also an [[individual]]: she is the only one holding a flag.

title: A dog at the gate
text: The poster shows a dog beside a child. Its tail is moving and its mouth is open, so the dog seems [[friendly]]. A large picture shows it near the gate. The caption uses simple [[language]]: “Come and meet your new friend.”

title: Mara the superhero
text: Mara is a superhero. She carries a map and leads the team through the rain. Her cape is bright red, so the [[colour]] is easy to notice. The picture shows her as [[strong]], but she also stops to help a child. This gives one clear [[idea]] about her.

title: The school play
text: Five students stand together after a play. They wear different [[clothing]], but they are one [[group]]. The camera shows their faces. They look [[serious]] because the story is about a storm.

title: Water the plant
text: A boy holds a watering can beside a small plant. The picture shows him looking after it. This is an [[example]] of a school message. The bright green [[colour]] helps the plant stand out.

title: A drummer’s hands
text: The [[camera]] shows a drummer playing a loud beat. The photo is close, so we can see the hands clearly. The musician wears a blue shirt. The picture makes the music look [[modern]].

title: The heavy box
text: A small robot tries to lift a box. Its arms shake, and it cannot move the box at first. The robot looks [[weak]]. Then a friend helps, and together they lift it. The poster shows a [[friendly]] team.

title: A music club advert
text: The advert shows a music club after school. A [[group]] of students plays together in the room. The room has bright lights and many colours. A short sentence invites students to join. The simple [[language]] makes the message easy to read.

title: A quiet portrait
text: A student sits by a window with a book. The [[camera]] shows a calm moment. The student’s face looks [[serious]], but the warm light makes the scene feel peaceful.

title: The park clean-up
text: A girl picks up a bottle in the park. She puts it in a bin, and another child helps. The poster shows a [[caring]] action. Both children are part of a [[group]] working together.

title: A bright birthday card
text: The card shows a cake beside three candles. Its main [[image]] is bright and easy to understand. The message says, “Have a lovely day!” The word “lovely” tells us the card is meant to feel [[friendly]].

title: A poster for a reading club
text: The poster shows a student reading under a lamp. The artist uses one small [[detail]]—a bookmark shaped like a rocket—to suggest that the story is exciting. The main [[image]] is easy to see because the background is plain. This design [[choice]] helps new readers understand the invitation quickly.

title: A mountain holiday advert
text: The advert shows a family beside a quiet lake, although it does not explain where the lake is. The warm light may create a feeling of comfort. A person looking at the image might think the holiday is expensive, but there is no clear [[reason]] in the advert—no price, hotel name, or travel details—to say that the family is [[wealthy]]. That is only a guess, since the advert gives no costs. The advert’s [[meaning]] depends on what viewers notice.

title: A school sports poster
text: The poster shows a runner near the finish line. Her raised arms make her look [[confident]], while the empty track keeps attention on her. The artist chose a bright [[colour]] for the number on her shirt. This helps viewers [[describe]] the main action without reading the small caption.

title: A toy advert
text: The advert shows a toy train moving through a painted forest. The forest is not [[realistic]], but its bright trees make the scene attractive to young children. One small [[detail]]—a smiling moon—adds humour. The designers [[create]] a playful mood rather than a picture of a real journey.

title: A portrait in the newspaper
text: The article shows a young inventor beside a table of tools. Her careful expression may [[suggest]] that she is concentrating, but it does not prove how she feels. The photograph gives readers a clear [[example]] of her work. A short caption helps [[explain]] why the invention matters to the school.

title: A café menu board
text: The café uses a hand-drawn picture of soup beside the menu. The picture makes the food seem warm and inviting. The large letters are easy to read from the door. This [[choice]] gives customers a clear [[reason]] to look at the board before they enter. The soup is the most noticeable [[detail]].

title: A comic-book cover
text: The cover shows a cyclist flying over a city. The scene is impossible, but it has a clear [[meaning]]: the character is moving quickly and freely. A low camera position makes the cyclist look [[powerful]]. The artist uses just one bright [[colour]] against a dark sky.

title: A poster about sleep
text: The poster shows a student putting a phone away before bed. The simple picture helps [[describe]] the action. A moon beside the clock is an important [[detail]]. A small arrow links the phone to a bedside drawer, making the action easy to follow. The main [[meaning]] is clear: a regular bedtime can help people feel rested, but the poster does not promise perfect sleep.

title: A travel photograph
text: A photograph shows a narrow path through a forest. The path leads the viewer’s eyes towards a small bridge. This [[choice]] can make the place seem peaceful. The photo gives no [[reason]] to assume that the path is safe, so the image alone cannot answer that question. Its quiet [[setting]] is easy to describe.

title: A school concert notice
text: The notice shows a violin and a drum beside the concert date. The instruments make the event easy to identify. A large heading gives the main [[idea]] first. The bright border helps [[create]] a cheerful mood without hiding the details families need. The date is an important [[detail]].

title: Two adverts for running shoes
text: The first advert shows a runner on an empty road at sunrise. The second places a group of friends on a track. To [[compare]] them, notice that the first focuses on one [[individual]], while the second emphasizes companionship. The sunrise may have a positive [[effect]] on the first advert’s mood. In the second, the friends’ smiles [[support]] a message about shared effort. Neither image proves that every runner prefers one style of exercise.

title: A headline about a student
text: A local paper uses the headline “Young inventor solves a city problem.” The article then describes a student who designed a rainwater collector for the school garden. The headline frames the student’s [[role]] as active and useful. A photograph of the working model provides [[evidence]] for the claim that the design was built. The report is mostly [[positive]], although it also mentions a leak that the student still needs to repair. This makes the account more [[realistic]] than a story that presents the project as perfect.

title: A costume in a school play
text: In the play, one character wears a plain grey [[costume]] and carries a bright yellow folder. The contrast makes the folder easy to notice. It may suggest that the character has important information, but the audience needs the dialogue to know what the folder contains. The actor’s [[pose]] is upright, which can communicate confidence. These choices [[support]] an interpretation of the character as prepared, though they do not tell us whether the character will succeed. The folder has a clear [[role]] in the scene: it carries the clue.

title: A wildlife charity leaflet
text: The leaflet shows a seal on a clean beach, then explains that plastic can harm sea animals. The first image creates a calm mood, while the facts describe a serious problem. The leaflet’s [[purpose]] is to encourage people to reduce waste. Its central claim is [[supported|support]] by examples of plastic found near the shore. The tone stays [[positive]] by including practical actions, such as using a refillable bottle. This balance makes the message more useful than a page that only tries to frighten readers. The intended [[audience]] is people who can change their daily habits.

title: A family in a television advert
text: The advert shows two adults preparing dinner while their child sets the table. The task is shared, so the scene does not present cooking as one person’s fixed [[role]]. A pan boils over, and someone laughs while wiping the counter. The kitchen looks [[ordinary]], and the camera shows small mistakes as well as the finished meal. This can make the scene feel more [[realistic]]. The advert may be challenging a [[traditional]] image of family life, but the evidence is limited to this one short scene.

title: A sports report
text: The report describes a close match and includes comments from players on both teams. One [[headline]] calls the final goal “unexpected,” while the photograph shows the scorer looking surprised. Together, these details [[support]] the idea that the result changed quickly. The article does not call either team lazy or weak. Its [[positive]] language helps readers focus on what happened rather than on an unfair judgment about the players. The photograph’s [[role]] is to show the scorer’s reaction.

title: A music video still
text: A still image shows a singer standing alone beneath a bright sign. The [[background]] is crowded with moving lights, but the singer remains sharply visible. This contrast may create a sense of isolation. The artist’s expression looks [[serious]], although a single frame cannot tell us exactly what the singer feels. The image gives viewers enough [[evidence]] to discuss the design, but not enough to explain the whole story of the song. The contrast has an emotional [[effect]] on viewers.

title: A poster about volunteering
text: The poster shows volunteers sorting books in a community room. It presents each person as an [[individual]] with a task, while the shelves and boxes show the scale of the project. The volunteers’ actions [[support]] the main message. A short caption explains how to join. This creates a stronger [[effect]] than a poster that only says “Be kind,” because viewers can see what the invitation asks them to do. The [[audience]] includes local people who might volunteer.

title: A documentary photograph
text: The photograph shows a mechanic repairing a bicycle outside a workshop. The [[setting]] gives the scene a practical feel, and the tools provide [[evidence]] of the work being done. The photographer does not show the whole repair, so viewers cannot know whether it was successful. Still, the image presents the mechanic as [[professional]] through careful attention to the task. That interpretation is supported by visible details rather than by the person’s appearance alone. These details may have a positive [[effect]] on the viewer.

title: A news story about a festival
text: The story includes a photograph of a crowded square and a short interview with an organiser. The image shows a large [[audience]], while the interview explains why the event was planned. A lively [[headline]] attracts attention, but the article also gives practical information about travel and noise. This mixture can create a more [[realistic]] account than a report that focuses only on excitement. Readers can use the details to understand both the celebration and its effect on nearby residents. The organiser’s [[response]] explains why the event was planned.

title: A campaign about public transport
text: The campaign uses a photograph of a nearly empty bus at dawn. A high [[camera angle]] makes the street seem wide, while the pale [[lighting]] gives the scene a quiet mood. The short [[slogan]] reads “Room to move.” Its [[purpose]] is to encourage commuters to try the early service, not to claim that every bus is empty. By including the timetable beside the photograph, the designers [[communicate]] a practical offer as well as an appealing atmosphere. The image may prompt a calm [[response]], but actual passengers could react differently.

title: A portrait of a young chef
text: The portrait places the chef in a busy kitchen, but the shallow focus keeps attention on her hands. Viewers can [[identify]] the work through the knife, vegetables and apron. Her [[facial expression]] is not fully visible, so the photograph does not tell us whether she is proud or tired. The [[pose]] suggests concentration because she is leaning towards the chopping board. The caption names her as the restaurant’s head chef, which helps [[present]] her expertise without relying on appearance. The article’s [[purpose]] is to introduce her work.

title: A game character design
text: The game introduces a guide who carries a map and asks the player to choose a route. The character’s [[body language]] is open: one hand points towards the path, while the other holds the map. This design may [[suggest]] that the guide is helpful, although the dialogue later gives stronger evidence. A warm [[colour]] separates the guide from the grey landscape. The designers [[communicate]] personality through several choices, rather than expecting one costume detail to explain the whole character. The guide’s main [[purpose]] is to help the player choose a route.

title: A museum exhibition poster
text: The poster combines a close-up of an old key with a wide view of a locked door. The [[contrast]] encourages viewers to connect a small object with a larger mystery. A low [[camera angle]] makes the door seem large beside the key. The designer uses a narrow column of text, so the event details remain easy to find. The poster’s [[target audience]] may include families who enjoy puzzles, but that reading is only a possibility. The age range and ticket information provide firmer [[evidence]] about whom the exhibition is designed to reach. Its [[purpose]] is to invite visitors to solve the mystery.

title: A food advert
text: The advert shows a bowl of noodles beside a window on a rainy day. Soft [[lighting]] makes the steam visible, and the camera uses a [[close-up]] to emphasize texture. The [[setting]] may invite viewers to associate the meal with comfort. The text does not say that the food will solve a difficult day; instead, the [[slogan]] promises a warm lunch. This is a narrower claim, and the image’s choices help [[support]] it.

title: A photo for a school council
text: The photograph shows one student speaking while several classmates listen. The camera is at eye level, giving the speaker equal visual status. The students’ [[pose]]—one leans towards the table while others take notes—suggests that the discussion matters. One student has raised a hand, and another is pointing to a page of notes. Their gestures and expressions also add to the scene. Their [[body language]] does not reveal what decision was made. The caption explains that the group is planning a quieter study area. This information helps viewers [[identify]] the photo as a record of a student meeting and understand the reason for the gathering. The photo’s [[purpose]] is to show how the council plans changes. The proposal may have a positive [[effect]] on students who need a quiet place.

title: A book cover redesign
text: The original cover uses a large face and a red title; the redesign shows a small house behind a field. The [[camera angle]] is wide, leaving plenty of space around the house. There is no person in the foreground to compete for attention, so the building becomes the first thing a reader notices. This new [[choice]] shifts attention from one person to the place where the story begins. The house and field establish the story’s [[setting]]. The grey sky suggests uncertainty, while the open gate offers another possibility; these details shape the first impression before a reader opens the book. The design [[presents|present]] the story as a mystery. These cues guide a reader’s first impression, but they do not summarize the plot. The publisher’s [[response]] to reader feedback was to keep the title clear and make the setting more prominent.

title: A road safety video
text: The video begins with a [[close-up]] of a phone lighting up in a car. The driver’s [[facial expression]] changes, and the camera then cuts to the road. This sequence makes the risk easy to understand without showing a crash. The narrator explains that a brief glance can remove a driver’s attention from traffic. The video’s [[purpose]] is to encourage safer habits; its [[effect]] depends partly on whether viewers remember the specific action it recommends. The closing [[slogan]] repeats that action in five words. The sound also becomes quiet when the phone lights up.

title: A profile of an inventor
text: The profile includes a photograph of an inventor at a workbench and a diagram of the finished device. The portrait makes the [[individual]] visible, while the diagram provides [[evidence]] of what the invention does. The article does not present success as instant: it describes several failed versions before the final design. This detail may [[challenge]] the idea that skilled people succeed without difficulty. The writer uses specific examples to [[support]] that interpretation, rather than treating one photograph as proof. The profile’s [[purpose]] is to explain how the device developed. A timeline shows when each version was tested.

title: A poster for a local play
text: The poster shows a character looking through a doorway, with most of the room hidden in shadow. This [[camera angle]] restricts what viewers can see and may create curiosity. A small line beneath the title gives the performance dates, so the dramatic design does not hide the practical information. The poster’s [[language]] is mysterious, but the text remains direct. The audience can [[identify]] the performance dates in the small line. The poster’s [[purpose]] is to attract viewers without revealing the secret. A viewer’s [[response]] may be curiosity.

title: Whose story leads the exhibition?
text: The exhibition opens with a large portrait of a bicycle courier, followed by smaller photographs of people who use the same streets. The courier occupies the [[foreground]] near the entrance, where visitors see this portrait before the street scenes. This [[choice]] gives the courier immediate prominence, but the later images complicate any assumption that the street belongs to one kind of person. A careful [[analysis]] distinguishes what the display shows from what a visitor might infer. The courier’s central position is visible [[evidence]]; the claim that the exhibition celebrates speed is less secure, since the labels focus on safety and access. The curator may [[imply]] that urban space is shared, without stating that argument directly.

title: A changing image of leadership
text: A company profile first shows its director beside a glass meeting table, framed by colleagues listening in silence. A later photograph places the same director among workers on the factory floor. The shift in [[setting]] changes the viewer’s vantage point across the two photographs; this may [[represent]] leadership as both formal and practical. It would be too strong to conclude that one photograph proves the director is approachable; the images construct a public [[identity]], while the interview supplies further evidence. Their [[contrast]] invites a more nuanced analysis of authority than either image could support alone. The accompanying interview offers additional [[evidence]].

title: The quiet character on the poster
text: The poster gives a supporting character only a narrow strip at the edge, although the character’s written message changes the plot. This difference between visual prominence and narrative importance is worth examining. The [[foreground]] is occupied by the protagonist, while the smaller figure remains partly in shadow. That arrangement may [[reinforce]] a familiar hierarchy of attention, yet it may also encourage viewers to search for overlooked details. The poster does not establish which interpretation its designers intended. A defensible account should connect its claims to precise [[evidence]] and leave room for uncertainty. The [[representation]] of the supporting character is visually limited. The caption gives the supporting character’s words in full. That quoted message shapes the character’s [[identity]] in the scene.

title: A familiar image reconsidered
text: The advertisement uses a polished kitchen and matching aprons, visual choices that could recall a [[stereotypical]] image of domestic life. However, the sequence shows different family members taking turns, and the final frame names the designer of the recipe as a child. These details [[challenge]] a simple reading of the advert as merely traditional. They do not erase the polished setting; instead, the text holds two ideas in tension. Its [[representation]] of family life is constructed through editing, captions and casting, rather than copied directly from everyday experience. The [[audience]] may use these details as [[evidence]] for a more complex reading.

title: A single frame, several claims
text: A photograph of a runner at the finish line appears in an article about a city marathon. The report is written for people who want to understand how the event was organised, not only who crossed the line first. Its [[audience]] may therefore notice details about route volunteers. The raised arms and open mouth may imply relief, excitement or exhaustion; none can be confirmed from the frame alone. The article’s caption identifies the runner as a volunteer who helped mark the route. This information changes the likely [[meaning]] of the image without changing its visible details. An analyst should [[contrast]] what the photograph makes available with what the caption adds, then explain how the two sources of information work together. A careful [[analysis]] keeps these sources distinct, and the caption provides [[evidence]] for the runner’s role. The article also names the route she helped mark and explains why it was closed to traffic.

title: Designing a less certain villain
text: The film poster shows a character in a dark coat, standing apart from the group. Those choices invite suspicion, but they do not make the character a villain by themselves. In the trailer, the character protects a younger neighbour and refuses to reveal why. The poster may [[imply]] danger, whereas the moving image introduces competing evidence. A strong [[analysis]] would identify both signals before deciding how the film [[presents|present]] the character. This approach avoids treating one visual convention as a fixed rule about personality. The film’s [[representation]] complicates a familiar [[stereotype]].

title: The missing voice in a news image
text: A report about a new building includes a photograph of the architect beside a model, but no image of the people who will use the space. The framing makes the design process visible while leaving its future occupants absent. The architect occupies the [[foreground]]. That omission may shape the article’s [[representation]] of success: the building is presented through its creator’s achievement. It does not prove that the journalist intended to exclude anyone. A reader can [[identify]] the imbalance in available viewpoints and ask what further [[evidence]] would be needed to assess its effect. The likely [[target audience]] includes people interested in city design.

title: A title that changes the reading
text: A photograph shows a person standing beside a closed shop with a hand-painted sign. The image itself does not indicate whether the shop is closing for the day or for good. The headline, “Last light on Market Street,” encourages a more final interpretation. Because the title supplies information the photograph cannot establish, a close [[analysis]] must consider both text and image. The headline may [[reinforce]] a sense of loss, while the visible sign offers no confirmation of the shop’s future. The headline gives a particular [[meaning]] to the scene. This title is also key [[evidence]] for the interpretation. The article says no closure date has been announced. Its [[purpose]] is to report on the uncertainty rather than to confirm a closure.

title: When a detail resists the main message
text: A campaign poster presents a runner against an empty road and uses the phrase “Go further alone.” The design appears to value independence, yet the small print thanks local volunteers who kept the route safe. This detail complicates the poster’s central [[idea]]: the activity is framed as individual achievement, although it depends on shared work. An [[audience]] may notice the tension differently, depending on whether attention falls first on the slogan or the acknowledgement. The campaign’s [[representation]] of achievement may [[reinforce]] an individual focus, although the small print supplies [[evidence]] of shared work.

title: How the image handles uncertainty
text: A portrait for a science article shows a researcher beside a display of data, but the chart is too small to read. The image establishes the researcher’s presence and the topic’s technical setting; it cannot verify the study’s findings. The caption supplies the result, while the article discusses limitations. A careful reader should [[contrast]] visual impression with factual support. The portrait may [[suggest]] expertise through its setting, but reliable claims about the research depend on accessible [[evidence]] and an accurate account of the method. A full [[analysis]] should also consider the likely [[target audience]].

title: Orange juice
text: A social media post shows a father making breakfast for his two children. He [[pours]] Sunny Days orange juice into three [[glasses]] while one child cuts toast. The caption says, “Start together.” The father is [[wearing]] an old T-shirt, and the [[kitchen]] looks like an ordinary family home.

title: Cold-pressed juice
text: Before a cinema film, a short advert shows a woman squeezing oranges by hand. She pours the [[juice]] into a clear [[bottle]] and gives it to a friend at a picnic. Soft music [[plays]]. The brand name appears on the bottle with the words “Made fresh each [[morning]].”

title: Breakfast cereal
text: A large billboard shows a boy in his school [[uniform]] eating cereal at the kitchen table. His mother sits beside him with her own [[bowl]]. Both are [[smiling]]. The cereal box is large in the corner, and the words “Ready for your day” appear [[across]] the top.

title: Boxed chocolates
text: In a short online video, a man [[opens]] a box of chocolates at home. He gives the first [[piece]] to his mother, who laughs and asks for another. The chocolates sit in a black box with a gold [[ribbon]]. The final [[screen]] says, “For someone special.”

title: Instant noodles
text: A billboard beside a bus stop shows a young woman eating noodles after a late [[shift]] at a shop. She still wears her work name [[badge]]. [[Steam]] rises from the bowl. The words “Dinner in three [[minutes]]” are big enough to read from across the road.

title: Meal kit
text: A website banner shows two friends preparing a meal together. One cuts [[vegetables]] while the other reads the [[recipe]] card from a meal kit. A picture of the [[finished]] dinner is beside them. A green button says “Choose your box,” and a smaller line shows the [[price]].

title: Supermarket coffee
text: Before a cinema film, an advert shows a supermarket worker making coffee in the staff room. She passes a cup to a [[colleague]] who has just [[arrived]]. They talk while the kettle cools. The [[packet]] appears on the table, followed by the words “A good start for [[everyone]].”

title: Speciality coffee
text: In a podcast advert, the host speaks about a small coffee shop she visited. She describes the [[smell]] of the beans and says that the owner [[remembers]] her name. We [[hear]] a cup being put on a table. At the end, she reads the speciality coffee brand’s website [[address]].

title: Sports drink
text: An online video follows a girl playing basketball with friends. She [[misses]] a [[shot]], drinks from a sports bottle and tries again. Her team [[cheers]] when the ball goes in. A fast beat plays as the bottle turns [[towards]] the camera. The final words are “Keep playing.”

title: Bottled water
text: In a radio advert, we hear shoes on a long path and someone [[breathing]] hard. A woman asks her walking [[partner]] if he has water. He [[opens]] a bottle and gives it to her. A voice then names the bottled water brand and says, “Take it [[with]] you.”

title: Everyday watch
text: A podcast host describes the everyday watch she [[wears]] to work. She says she can read its large [[numbers]] when her hands are full. We hear a bus door [[close]] as she talks about getting to school on [[time]]. The brand name and shop address come at the end.

title: Luxury watch
text: A black and gold billboard shows a man alone on a yacht. He wears a dark suit and looks at a luxury watch on his [[wrist]]. The watch is bright, but his face is in [[shadow]]. The words “Your time has come” appear [[beside]] the brand name. No [[price]] is shown.

title: School trainers
text: An online video shows a child putting on school trainers without help. The shoes have wide [[straps]]. She runs to meet her friends at the school [[gate]], then stops to [[tie]] one friend’s loose lace. The final shot shows the trainers in three [[colours]] with the words “Ready every morning.”

title: Designer trainers
text: Before a film at the cinema, a designer trainer advert shows a dancer [[practising]] alone in a large, empty studio. She [[repeats]] the same move [[until]] she gets it right. The trainers are shown close up when her feet [[land]]. A deep voice says, “Make your own mark.”

title: Waterproof coat
text: A sponsored social post shows an older woman walking her dog in [[heavy]] rain. Water runs off her waterproof coat, but the [[shirt]] under it stays dry. She smiles at another dog [[walker]]. The caption says, “Rain is still a good day,” with a [[link]] to three coat colours.

title: Designer coat
text: A radio advert begins with music and the sound of people [[entering]] a party. A woman asks who [[designed]] a guest’s coat. The guest gives the designer’s name, and the room becomes [[quiet]] for a moment. A voice says the coat is available by [[appointment]] at one city shop.

title: Basic handbag
text: Before a cinema film, a basic handbag advert shows a woman leaving home with a bag full of [[books]]. At work, she [[takes]] out a lunch box. Later, she [[carries]] the same bag to the park. The final shot shows its [[price]] beside the words “One bag for your day.”

title: Designer handbag
text: An online video shows a designer handbag being made. A worker cuts the leather, another [[sews]] the [[handle]], and a woman checks the finished bag in a [[mirror]]. She walks into a gallery opening. There is no voiceover. The brand name appears in small [[letters]] on a white screen.

title: Everyday fragrance
text: A billboard shows a teenager [[spraying]] an everyday fragrance before meeting friends in the park. The friends [[wave]] when he arrives. The [[bottle]] stands beside him in the picture. Bright colours surround the words “Feel ready to go,” and a small price appears [[below]] the bottle.

title: Luxury perfume
text: A podcast advert begins with the host describing the [[smell]] of flowers in her grandmother’s garden. She says a luxury perfume [[reminds]] her of that place. Soft piano music plays [[behind]] her voice. She names the perfume and says it can be [[tried]] at a small number of shops.

title: Budget smartphone
text: A poster inside a train shows a student holding a budget smartphone and [[checking]] the next [[stop]]. The screen is bright and easy to see. Another student beside him looks at the same [[map]]. The [[price]] is in large letters, with the words “Everything you need to get there.”

title: Flagship smartphone
text: A billboard shows a woman standing on a city [[roof]] at night. She holds a flagship phone towards the lights below. The camera [[lenses]] are large in the picture. The words “See more after dark” sit beside a [[photograph]] she has taken. No price appears on the [[board]].

title: Language-learning app
text: In a television advert for a language app, a new student says “hello” to a neighbour in another language. At first she speaks [[slowly]]. The neighbour smiles and [[answers]]. A phone screen shows a short [[lesson]], then the words “Five minutes a day” and a green [[download]] button.

title: Gaming headphones
text: A website banner for gaming headphones shows two friends playing a game in [[different]] homes. One speaks into the [[microphone]], and the other laughs before moving her character. Bright lines [[connect]] their screens. A button below the picture says “Hear your team,” beside the headphones and their [[price]].

title: Premium noise-cancelling headphones
text: A radio advert begins with traffic, a [[barking]] dog and a loud train. The sounds grow [[softer]] as a man puts on premium noise-cancelling headphones. We then hear him say, “Now I can [[think]].” A calm voice names the brand and tells [[listeners]] where to try the headphones.

title: Family tablet
text: A podcast host describes how her children use a family tablet. One [[watches]] a drawing lesson while the other [[reads]] a story. She says they have [[separate]] profiles, so each child sees their own work. The host then gives the tablet’s name and a link to its [[website]].

title: Professional camera
text: A radio advert begins with a camera [[clicking]] three times. A woman describes taking photographs of a dancer on a dark [[stage]]. She says she can still see the dancer’s face [[clearly]]. The professional camera’s name follows, along with an [[invitation]] to try it at a specialist shop.

title: Fitness tracker
text: A sponsored social post shows a middle-aged man walking up [[stairs]] at work. His fitness tracker [[counts]] each step. In the next picture, his daughter [[joins]] him for a walk after dinner. The caption says, “Every step belongs to you,” and invites [[viewers]] to set a daily goal.

title: Home security system
text: A poster on a station platform shows a woman [[checking]] the home security app on her [[phone]]. On the screen, a camera shows her front [[door]] and a [[parcel]] beside it. The train arrives behind her. The words “See home from anywhere” sit above a picture of the camera.

title: Entry-level laptop
text: A magazine advert shows a girl using an entry-level laptop at a small [[desk]]. She is making a [[poster]] for her school club. The laptop screen is large in the picture, and the price is [[printed]] below it. The line “Make your first big idea” appears at the [[top]].

title: Family car
text: A poster inside a bus shows a family car parked beside a football field. A mother takes a ball from the [[boot]] while her son helps his [[younger]] sister out. There are bags and [[coats]] in the car. The poster says, “Room for every Saturday,” with a price at the [[bottom]].

title: Luxury car
text: A podcast host describes arriving at a hotel in a luxury car. She speaks about the quiet [[ride]] and the driver [[opening]] the door for her. We hear the door close softly. The brand name comes at the end, [[followed]] by an invitation to [[book]] a private test drive.

title: City bicycle
text: In a television advert, a woman rides a city bicycle to the [[market]]. She puts vegetables in a [[basket]] at the front. On the way [[home]], she stops to talk to a [[neighbour]]. The bike stands beside them. The words “Your town, your way” appear with the shop’s name.

title: Racing bicycle

The camera stays close to the bicycle’s [[wheels]]. The final screen gives the bike’s name and racing team.

title: Budget hotel stay
text: An online video shows a man entering a budget hotel with two [[children]]. They put their [[bags]] down, look out at the city and make a [[plan]] for the day. The room [[price]] appears clearly on screen. A button below the video says, “Find a room near you.”

title: Luxury hotel stay
text: A full-page magazine advert shows a woman [[reading]] beside a private [[pool]] at a luxury hotel. A worker places a drink on her table. The [[sea]] is visible beyond the pool. The hotel name is printed in small gold [[letters]] with the words “Your time, entirely yours.”

title: Household vacuum cleaner
text: In a radio advert, we hear a vacuum cleaner and a child [[asking]] if she can help. Her father shows her how to move it [[across]] the carpet. The sound [[stops]], and they both laugh. A voice gives the household vacuum’s price and says it is available at local [[stores]].

title: Flat-pack sofa
text: A sponsored social post shows two flat-pack sofa [[boxes]] arriving at a shared flat. Three friends carry them upstairs, [[build]] the sofa and sit down to watch a film. The caption says, “Made for your first place.” A link opens a page with the price and [[assembly]] [[instructions]].

title: Designer sofa
text: A website banner shows a designer sofa in a large room with tall [[windows]]. An older couple sits at [[opposite]] ends while a [[grandchild]] reads between them. The sofa’s shape is shown clearly from the side. A button says, “Explore the [[collection]],” but no price appears.

title: Shampoo

title: Premium skincare serum
text: A station poster shows a close view of a woman putting a [[drop]] of premium skincare serum on her hand. She has visible [[lines]] around her eyes and smiles at the camera. The bottle stands [[beside]] her. The words “Care for the skin you live in” appear [[without]] a price.

title: Mobile data plan
text: A website banner shows a family speaking to a [[grandparent]] on a video call. The mobile data plan’s [[monthly]] price is beside the screen. One child holds up a [[drawing]] for the grandparent to see. A blue button says, “Choose your plan,” and the small print gives the data [[amount]].

title: Private tutoring service
text: A sponsored social post shows a boy and a private tutor working at a kitchen [[table]]. He [[explains]] an answer while the tutor listens and nods. The caption says, “His ideas, his voice.” A link offers an introductory [[meeting]], and the tutor’s [[qualifications]] appear below the photo.

title: Gym membership
text: A television advert shows a woman entering a gym for the first time. She looks unsure, but a [[trainer]] shows her where to put her [[bag]] and how to use a [[machine]]. Other people are exercising nearby. The words “Start where you are” appear with the monthly [[membership]] price.

title: Wellness retreat
text: A television advert for a wellness retreat opens with [[traffic]] and phone sounds. A man arrives at a quiet [[house]] in the hills and [[puts]] his phone away. He walks beside a [[lake]] with a guide. At the end, the retreat’s name and the dates of a three-day visit appear.

title: Children’s board game
text: A website banner shows children sitting around a board game. One girl reads a card [[aloud]] while the others laugh and move their [[pieces]]. A parent sits [[nearby]] but does not play for them. The game box, age [[range]] and price appear next to a button marked “See how to play.”

title: Collectable toy set
text: A magazine advert shows a collectable toy robot inside a clear [[case]]. A young adult [[collector]] checks its number on a small card. Other numbered toys stand on a [[shelf]] behind her. The line “Complete your collection” appears beneath the product, with the release [[date]] in small print.

title: Streaming subscription
text: A magazine advert shows a family [[choosing]] a film on their television. A grandmother picks one [[title]], and her grandson picks another. The streaming service’s [[logo]] appears on both screens. The [[monthly]] price and the words “Something for everyone tonight” sit at the bottom of the page.

title: Premium bank account
text: A magazine advert for a premium bank account shows a woman entering an airport [[lounge]]. She carries a small [[suitcase]] and a work bag. A staff member [[greets]] her by name. The account’s monthly fee appears in small [[print]] under the words “Every journey considered.”

title: Orange juice
text: A banner on a cooking website shows two sisters making breakfast for their father. The older girl pours orange juice, while the younger one carries the glasses [[carefully]] to the table. Their father is still [[wearing]] his work clothes. A line [[beneath]] the picture says, “A little help makes the morning brighter.” The [[carton]], price and a “Shop now” button appear on the right.

title: Cold-pressed juice
text: A billboard for cold-pressed juice shows a man [[leaving]] an early exercise class. He sits on the [[steps]] outside and drinks from a glass bottle while other people walk past with coffee. The picture uses soft morning light, and the [[label]] lists the fruit inside. The line “Take the morning slowly” appears above the bottle, but no price is [[printed]].

title: Breakfast cereal
text: In a sponsored social post, a father makes breakfast before his children [[wake]] up. He leaves three [[bowls]] of cereal at their places and puts a note beside each one. The youngest child finds a [[drawing]] of a dinosaur on hers. The caption says, “A good morning starts with knowing them.” The cereal box and a supermarket [[link]] appear below the video.

title: Boxed chocolates
text: A poster inside a train shows a woman [[holding]] a box of chocolates on her way to visit an old friend. She looks at a [[photograph]] of them as teenagers on her phone. The box is [[wrapped]] in pale blue paper, and the brand name appears in silver [[letters]]. The line “For the stories you still share” sits above a small image of the chocolates.

title: Instant noodles
text: A magazine advert for instant noodles shows a student coming home after a long evening at the [[library]]. His flatmate is already at the table, finishing an [[assignment]]. He makes two [[bowls]] and puts one beside her laptop. The page is bright and crowded, with the words “Three minutes. Two tired friends.” The price and two available [[flavours]] appear in the corner.

title: Meal kit
text: Before a cinema film, a meal-kit advert follows a couple preparing dinner with their teenage daughter. She takes the [[lead]], reading the [[recipe]] and giving each adult a job. When they sit down, she asks them to [[taste]] her sauce first. The voiceover says, “Dinner is better when everyone has a part.” The box, [[weekly]] price and ordering website appear at the end.

title: Supermarket coffee
text: A sponsored social post shows a supermarket [[cashier]] taking a coffee [[break]] with a colleague. They sit outside the store in ordinary uniforms, [[sharing]] biscuits from a paper bag. The post has no celebrity or perfect kitchen. Its caption says, “Good coffee for the days that start early.” The packet and price are shown [[clearly]], followed by a link to the supermarket.

title: Speciality coffee
text: During a podcast, the host describes visiting a coffee grower and watching the beans being [[sorted]]. We [[hear]] birds and people talking behind her voice. She says the speciality coffee has a bright [[taste]] and explains how she makes it at home. The grower’s name and the brand’s website are read [[aloud]] at the end, along with the price of a trial bag.

title: Sports drink
text: A radio advert begins with the sounds of a school running club. Trainers hit the [[track]], and several young people [[cheer]] each other on. One girl stops for a drink before going back to help a friend [[finish]]. The [[narrator]] says the sports drink is “for every kind of finish.” A shop name and the price of a bottle close the advert.

title: Bottled water
text: Before a cinema film, a bottled-water advert follows a night worker leaving a hospital as the sun [[rises]]. She drinks from a bottle while waiting for a bus and smiles when her son sends her a [[message]]. There is little [[dialogue]]. The music grows warmer as the bus arrives, and the final [[screen]] shows the bottle with the words “Take care of your day.”

title: Everyday watch
text: A sponsored post shows an everyday watch on the [[wrists]] of three people. A [[chef]] checks it before opening a café, a parent checks it outside a school, and a teenager checks it before a bus arrives. Each is shown doing an ordinary task. The caption reads, “Time for the things you do.” The watch’s price and three [[strap]] colours appear [[below]].

title: Luxury watch
text: A magazine advert shows a woman in a [[tailored]] suit standing alone in an empty concert hall. She checks a luxury watch before stepping onto the stage to [[conduct]] an orchestra. The [[audience]] has not arrived yet. Gold light falls on the watch, while her face stays partly in [[shadow]]. The line “Before they see you” appears above the brand name, with no price.

title: School trainers
text: Before a cinema film, an advert follows two children walking to school in the same style of trainers. One child runs [[ahead]], while the other moves more slowly with a walking aid. They meet at the school [[gate]] and [[compare]] the colours of their shoes. The line “Different mornings. Same way in” appears [[beside]] the trainers, their price and the shop name.

title: Designer trainers
text: A podcast host describes watching a street dancer practise for a performance. She says the dancer wore designer trainers and kept [[repeating]] a difficult step after everyone else had left. A short [[recording]] of the music plays [[beneath]] the story. The host then names the designer and gives the date when the limited shoes become available. The price is [[mentioned]] at the end.

title: Waterproof coat
text: In an online video, a father and daughter walk to school through heavy rain. The daughter wears a waterproof coat, but the father has only an [[umbrella]] that keeps turning inside out. They laugh when she offers him her [[hood]]. At the gate, she takes off the coat and shows that her [[uniform]] is dry. The video ends with three [[sizes]] and a clear price.

title: Designer coat
text: A billboard shows a designer coat hanging on the back of a [[chair]] in an empty theatre. Beyond it, an actor stands on stage during a [[rehearsal]]. The coat’s red lining is the only strong colour in the picture. The words “An [[entrance]] worth making” sit beside the brand name. There is no model [[wearing]] it and no price on the billboard.

title: Basic handbag
text: A magazine page shows a care worker carrying a basic handbag on a bus. Inside are a lunch box, house keys, a [[notebook]] and a small gift for someone she visits. The advert uses four close pictures to show each [[pocket]]. Its main line says, “Room for the whole day.” The bag is shown in two [[colours]], with the price printed clearly [[underneath]].

title: Designer handbag
text: A double-page magazine advert for a designer handbag shows an older woman and her adult daughter standing in a [[lift]]. They each [[carry]] the same style in a different colour. The daughter smiles at the [[mirror]], while the mother looks towards the open door. The line “Never just one story” appears across the pages. The bags and brand name are shown without [[prices]].

title: Everyday fragrance
text: A social media video shows a teenage boy getting ready for his first day at a new college. He puts on an everyday fragrance, then stops at the door and checks his [[timetable]] again. A [[classmate]] later invites him to sit with a group. The caption says, “Feel ready for the first hello.” The bottle and an [[affordable]] price appear beside a shop [[link]].

title: Luxury perfume
text: A sponsored post for a luxury perfume shows a woman getting ready for an awards dinner. She takes off her [[jewellery]], changes into a plain black dress and adds the perfume last. The camera stays close to her hands [[rather]] than showing the other guests. The [[caption]] reads, “What remains when everything else is quiet.” The bottle appears on a dark [[background]] with no price.

title: Budget smartphone
text: In a radio advert, a man explains that he needs a phone for calls, messages and taking pictures of his [[grandchildren]]. We hear him ask a shop worker [[whether]] the budget smartphone can do those things. She answers each question [[plainly]] and gives the price. At the end, his granddaughter laughs at the first photo he sends her, and the brand name is [[repeated]].

title: Flagship smartphone
text: A television advert shows a woman [[recording]] a street [[musician]] at night on a flagship smartphone. She sends the video to her brother, who is watching from another city. The camera cuts [[between]] her bright screen and his dark living room. A [[voiceover]] says, “Bring them closer to what you see.” The phone appears in several colours, while the price is left off screen.

title: Language-learning app
text: A banner on a travel website shows a woman arriving at a small restaurant in another country. Her phone [[displays]] a short lesson from a language app, and she [[orders]] her meal using a new [[phrase]]. The server answers and she smiles, then asks him to [[repeat]] the last word. A green “Try a free lesson” button appears below the app logo.

title: Gaming headphones
text: A radio advert begins with two friends speaking during an online game. One cannot hear the other over the [[noise]] from his room, so he puts on gaming headphones and asks her to say the plan again. We hear her voice [[clearly]] this time. The narrator names the microphone [[feature]] and gives the price, followed by a short line from the friends [[celebrating]] together.

title: Premium noise-cancelling headphones
text: A television advert follows a man [[commuting]] across a noisy city. On the train, he puts on premium noise-cancelling headphones, and the traffic sound [[fades]]. He can still hear an [[announcement]] when he chooses a different setting. The final shot shows him arriving at a rehearsal with his [[violin]]. The voiceover says, “Choose what gets through,” and the product name appears.

title: Family tablet
text: A television advert shows a family tablet being used at three different times. In the morning, a child reads a story. Later, his sister [[draws]] a map, and their grandmother joins a video call in the evening. Each person opens a separate [[profile]]. The closing screen shows the tablet beside the words “A place for everyone,” with its [[storage]] size and price [[below]].

title: Professional camera
text: A podcast host describes photographing a school play with a professional camera. She could not move close to the stage, but she says the faces were still clear in her pictures. We hear the curtain open and the [[audience]] clap. She names the [[lens]] she used and explains that the camera can be [[tested]] at a local shop. The price is [[available]] online.

title: Fitness tracker
text: An online video shows a fitness tracker on the wrist of a woman who works at a [[desk]]. When it [[reminds]] her to move, she walks downstairs and meets a neighbour outside. Later, they begin taking short walks together. The screen shows [[steps]] rather than [[weight]]. At the end, a line reads, “A little movement can lead somewhere,” next to the tracker’s price.

title: Home security system
text: A radio advert begins with a [[doorbell]] while a family is away. A home security camera sends an [[alert]] to the mother’s phone, and she sees a delivery driver leaving a [[parcel]]. She tells her partner that it has arrived. The narrator explains the camera and monthly service fee, then says the family can check the door from anywhere with a [[connection]].

title: Entry-level laptop
text: A website banner shows an entry-level laptop at a kitchen table. A father uses it to [[apply]] for a job, while his daughter waits to finish her school [[project]]. The two screens appear side by side to show that the laptop can [[handle]] both tasks. The price is large and a blue [[button]] says, “See what it can do.”

title: Family car
text: A television advert shows a family car outside a swimming pool. Two fathers [[load]] towels and bags into the boot while their children [[argue]] about who won the race. The children climb in, still wearing wet hair. The voiceover says, “There’s room for the whole story.” The final shot shows the number of [[seats]], the price and the car in three [[colours]].

title: Luxury car
text: In a podcast advert, the host describes [[being]] driven to a meeting in a luxury car. She remembers the quiet inside, even when the road outside was [[crowded]]. Her guest asks [[whether]] the car made her less nervous. She laughs and says it gave her time to [[prepare]]. The brand name follows, with an invitation to arrange a private test drive.

title: City bicycle
text: A poster in a station shows a woman cycling to work in ordinary clothes. She stops at a [[crossing]] beside people walking and takes a [[folded]] jacket from her basket. The city bicycle is shown from the side, with a map of nearby cycle [[paths]] underneath. The line “The short way across town” appears above a price and a shop [[address]].

title: Racing bicycle
text: A racing bicycle billboard shows a rider [[reaching]] the top of a hill at dawn. Another rider, much older, is close behind her. Both are shown working hard, and neither appears to be winning. The [[frame]] and [[wheels]] are lit clearly. The words “Keep finding another climb” appear beside a team [[logo]], but the price is not shown.

title: Budget hotel stay
text: A poster inside a train shows three friends checking into a budget hotel after a concert. One carries a guitar [[case]] and another has fallen [[asleep]] on her feet. They see the room price on a screen at [[reception]] and laugh with [[relief]]. The poster says, “A bed when the music ends,” followed by a map showing the hotel near the station.

title: Luxury hotel stay
text: A podcast host describes a luxury hotel where a worker [[noticed]] her mother found [[stairs]] difficult. The worker showed them a room close to the lift without being asked. The host speaks about the sea view too, but returns to that small act of [[care]]. Soft music plays before the hotel name and a booking address are read [[aloud]].

title: Household vacuum cleaner
text: An online video for a household [[vacuum]] cleaner shows a family tidying up after a birthday party. The teenage son begins the cleaning while his father takes down [[decorations]]. A close shot follows crumbs disappearing from under a table. The child who had the birthday falls [[asleep]] on the sofa. The last screen gives the [[price]] and the words “Ready for tomorrow.”

title: Premium robot vacuum
text: Before a cinema film, a premium robot vacuum moves through a busy home. A woman watches it turn around her father’s walking [[stick]] rather than [[bumping]] into it. Later, he moves the chair so it can clean [[underneath]]. The camera follows both people as they make space for the machine. The advert ends with the app [[controls]] and a premium price.

title: Flat-pack sofa
text: A banner on a furniture website shows three flat-pack sofa boxes arriving at a small apartment. A woman and her brother [[build]] the sofa together, [[following]] pictures on a sheet. The next image shows them sitting on it with their dog [[between]] them. The words “Your place, your hands” appear next to the price and an [[assembly]] video button.

title: Designer sofa
text: A designer sofa billboard shows a grandmother sitting with her grandson on a long green sofa. He is [[teaching]] her a card game, and the cards are [[spread]] between them. The room is simple, with a large [[window]] and almost no other furniture. The line “Space for what matters” appears in small letters beside the [[brand]] name. There is no price.

title: Shampoo
text: A magazine advert for shampoo shows a woman after swimming practice. She wears a team jacket and carries a bag with wet [[towels]]. In the second picture, she [[washes]] her hair at home before joining friends for dinner. The bottle stands [[between]] the images. The words “From one part of your day to the next” appear beside a clear shop [[price]].

title: Premium skincare serum
text: A website banner for premium skincare serum shows a woman in her [[sixties]] looking directly at the camera. The photograph leaves the lines on her face [[visible]]. Beside it, a close shot shows her using a small amount of serum. The line “Care that begins with your skin” sits above an [[ingredients]] link and a [[button]] to see the price.

title: Mobile data plan
text: Before a cinema film, a mobile data plan advert follows a son sending short videos to his mother while [[travelling]]. She watches him cross a bridge, then [[replies]] with a video of the family dog at home. The voiceover says, “Keep sharing the small things.” The [[monthly]] price and data [[limit]] appear on screen long enough to read.

title: Private tutoring service
text: In an online video, a private tutor meets a student who can explain an idea [[aloud]] but [[struggles]] to write it down. She listens first, then asks him to turn one sentence into a [[paragraph]]. He reads it back to her with a smile. The advert gives the tutor’s experience and lesson price at the end, followed by a [[booking]] link.

title: Gym membership
text: A gym membership billboard shows a woman in work clothes standing beside a weight machine. A [[trainer]] explains how to set it, and a second photograph shows her trying it [[herself]]. Other members look busy with their own exercises. The line “Nobody starts as an [[expert]]” sits above the monthly [[fee]] and the gym’s opening hours.

title: Wellness retreat
text: A poster inside a train shows a woman [[arriving]] at a wellness retreat with a suitcase and a work laptop. In the next picture, the laptop is [[closed]] while she joins a group walk. The line “Leave room for yourself” appears above the retreat’s [[dates]]. The poster also lists the [[cost]] of the three-day stay in small print.

title: Children’s board game
text: In a radio advert for a children’s board game, we hear a child reading a card [[aloud]]. Her uncle chooses the [[wrong]] answer and everyone laughs. A voice explains that players work in [[teams]], then gives the game’s age [[range]] and price. The sound of the final card being turned closes the advert before the brand name.

title: Collectable toy set
text: A television advert shows a collectable toy set on a [[shelf]] in a teenager’s room. She carefully opens a new figure, reads its [[numbered]] card and places it next to older ones. Her younger brother asks why she keeps the boxes. She explains which picture [[belongs]] to each figure. The advert ends with the [[release]] date and a shop list.

title: Streaming subscription
text: A poster on a station [[platform]] shows a father and daughter choosing different [[programmes]] on a streaming service. He watches a cooking show on his phone, while she watches a cartoon on a tablet. They put the screens away when their train arrives. The monthly price and number of available [[profiles]] are printed [[below]] the words “Your journey, your choice.”

title: Premium bank account
text: An online video for a premium bank account follows a business owner arriving late at an airport. She calls the account’s travel [[support]] service and gets help changing her [[booking]]. The advert shows the call rather than a luxury lounge. The final screen lists the monthly fee and travel [[benefit]], with a link to the full account [[terms]].

title: Orange juice
text: A poster inside a train shows a young delivery worker drinking orange juice while he waits for the first service of the morning. His bicycle is beside him, and his phone displays several [[addresses]]. Across the poster, the words “A fresh start for every shift” appear in orange. The [[carton]] and a low price are printed near the route map. Other passengers are [[blurred]] behind him, so the worker and the drink are the first things [[commuters]] notice.

title: Cold-pressed juice
text: On another train platform, a cold-pressed juice poster shows a woman in running clothes beside a man wearing office clothes. They each hold the same glass bottle, but stand at [[opposite]] ends of the image. The [[label]] names the fruit and the date the juice was made. A narrow line of text reads, “However your day begins.” The price is [[absent]], and the platform’s grey walls make the green bottles look [[especially]] bright.

title: Breakfast cereal
text: A breakfast cereal billboard shows a mother leaving home for a night shift as her partner [[prepares]] breakfast for their son. She takes a small [[bowl]] with her while the boy sits at the table. Both adults wear work clothes, and nobody speaks in the photograph. The [[tagline]] reads, “Morning happens at different times.” A large cereal box fills the right-hand side, with a supermarket price [[printed]] below the family.

title: Boxed chocolates
text: Before a cinema screening, a boxed-chocolate advert shows a father visiting his adult daughter in a new apartment. He has wrapped the chocolates himself, but the ribbon is [[uneven]]. She opens the box, [[recognises]] the brand and offers him the first piece. The camera pauses on their hands [[rather]] than their faces. Soft music plays as the words “For the moments you make” appear beside the product and an online shop [[address]].

title: Instant noodles
text: A podcast host describes an instant-noodle dinner she shared with her younger brother after helping him move into a student room. He had no plates, so they ate from the bowls in the kitchen box. We hear the [[kettle]] click and the two of them laughing. She reads the packet’s price and [[preparation]] time, then names the supermarket where it is [[sold]]. The story presents a cheap meal as part of a new [[beginning]].

title: Meal kit
text: In a radio advert for a meal kit, a woman tells her partner she wants to cook for friends but has never made the dish on the menu. We hear vegetables being [[chopped]] while the kit’s recipe is read [[aloud]] between their jokes. The friends [[arrive]] just as the oven sounds. A narrator explains what comes in each box, states the price for two or four people and gives a website for [[choosing]] next week’s meals.

title: Supermarket coffee
text: A sponsored social post for supermarket coffee shows four workers finishing different late [[shifts]]. A cleaner, a driver, a nurse and a shop worker each make a cup at home before they sleep. The pictures use warm kitchen light but leave their [[uniforms]] visible. The [[caption]] reads, “For every kind of morning,” followed by the packet price. Comments from customers describe when they drink it, and the supermarket [[replies]] with its opening times.

title: Speciality coffee
text: A speciality-coffee billboard outside an office building shows a [[grower]] standing [[among]] coffee plants, holding a small bag with his name on it. Beside him, a barista in the city serves a cup made from those beans. A thin line [[connects]] the two photographs. The copy reads, “Know where your morning begins.” The café’s [[address]] appears clearly, while the price is printed much smaller near the bottom.

title: Sports drink
text: A magazine advert for a sports drink shows a teenage wheelchair basketball player practising after her teammates have left. A coach passes her the ball, and she takes another [[shot]]. The bottle stands on the floor beside her chair, within [[reach]]. The headline says, “The work nobody sees.” The drink’s [[ingredients]] and price appear in a small panel, while the full-page photograph gives most of its space to her [[concentration]].

title: Bottled water
text: An online video for bottled water follows a grandfather teaching his grandson how to [[plant]] vegetables. They take a break in the [[shade]] and share water from two bottles. The boy asks why they must wait for the seeds to grow, and the grandfather laughs. The [[voiceover]] says, “Good things take time.” The bottles appear on a garden table, and the final screen lists the price and shops [[selling]] them.

title: Everyday watch
text: An online advert for an everyday watch shows a woman who manages the morning school run with her sister. One prepares breakfast while the other takes the children to the bus stop. They check [[identical]] watches as they pass keys [[between]] them. The video uses quick cuts but no dramatic music. The final line reads, “Made for days you share,” followed by a large price, a [[warranty]] line and three available [[strap]] colours.

title: Luxury watch
text: A luxury-watch billboard shows an older [[architect]] alone in her studio at night. Models of buildings surround her, and the city beyond the window is dark. She turns a watch in her hands before putting it on. A narrow [[beam]] of light catches its [[face]]. The words “Time leaves a mark” sit under the brand name. Nothing on the board identifies a price or explains [[whether]] the watch is connected to her work.

title: School trainers
text: A radio advert for school trainers begins with a child asking her father [[whether]] she can walk to school on her own. We hear the front door close and her shoes move along different streets. She meets a friend at the [[crossing]] and they arrive together. The father’s voice says she is growing up quickly. The narrator names the trainers, mentions their strong [[straps]] and gives a price [[available]] in several shops.

title: Designer trainers
text: A designer-trainer billboard shows a young man on a stage after a dance performance. His hands are still shaking, and he is not looking at the [[audience]]. [[Instead]], he watches the younger dancer who has come up beside him. Their trainers [[match]] but their clothes do not. The line “The next step is yours” runs between them. The designer logo is large, while the release date and [[stockists]] appear in small text.

title: Waterproof coat
text: A waterproof-coat billboard outside a station shows two grandparents and their grandson walking through heavy rain. The child splashes ahead while the adults carry shopping bags. All three wear the same coat in different sizes. A close [[inset]] shows water running off a [[sleeve]]. The line “The weather doesn’t choose your age” appears above a price [[range]]. The muddy path and wet shopping bags make the scene look like an [[ordinary]] trip home.

title: Designer coat
text: Before a cinema film, a designer-coat advert opens with a [[tailor]] drawing a [[pattern]] in a quiet workshop. An older male model tries the finished coat, then passes a mirror to a younger woman wearing a version of the same design. Both look at their own [[reflections]] rather than each other. Piano music plays as the camera moves over the [[stitching]]. The brand name and the words “Made to be kept” appear without a price.

title: Basic handbag
text: A television advert follows a young care worker carrying a basic handbag between three homes. She takes out keys, a [[notebook]] and a birthday card for one of the people she [[visits]]. At the end of the day she places the bag beside her own kitchen table. A [[voiceover]] calls it “a place for everything you carry.” The price appears clearly on screen, while the people she helps are shown speaking with her rather than waiting [[silently]].

title: Designer handbag
text: In a radio advert for a designer handbag, a woman describes finding her mother’s old bag at the back of a [[cupboard]]. The leather has marks from use, but she remembers carrying it to her first job [[interview]]. A second voice explains that the brand [[repairs]] older pieces. We hear the [[clasp]] click shut. The advert ends with the name of the repair service and an invitation to make a private appointment.

title: Everyday fragrance
text: An online video for an everyday fragrance shows a boy preparing for a school dance. He tries several shirts, chooses the one he already [[owns]] and uses a little fragrance before leaving. At the dance, he spends more time helping a [[nervous]] friend than trying to [[impress]] anyone. The final screen says, “Feel like yourself,” beside the bottle and its price. The music is light and the party looks small enough to feel [[familiar]].

title: Luxury perfume
text: Before a film, a luxury-perfume advert follows a woman through an empty museum after closing. She stops before a painting of a person [[whose]] face is turned away, then takes a small bottle from her bag. The [[scent]] is never described. Deep blue lighting and slow [[strings]] shape the mood. The brand name appears over the painting at the end, with the words “Leave something unseen.” There is no price or information about [[ingredients]].

title: Budget smartphone
text: A television advert shows a budget smartphone passing between three members of one family. A grandmother calls her son, he checks a recipe, and his daughter uses the camera for a school project. Each person changes one [[setting]] to suit them. The phone is shown clearly rather than [[hidden]] in their hands. The voiceover names the [[battery]] life and [[storage]], then states the price. A final shot shows the family sitting together without screens.

title: Flagship smartphone
text: A banner on a photography website shows a flagship smartphone taking a picture of a musician under [[streetlights]]. A second image displays the photograph in close detail, with the musician’s face still [[visible]]. The photographer is a woman wearing a work uniform who has stopped on her way home. The line “Keep what catches your eye” appears above a button [[labelled]] “Explore the camera.” The phone’s price [[requires]] another click.

title: Language-learning app
text: A sponsored social post shows a teenage girl using a language-learning app before meeting her grandfather’s friends. She practises a [[greeting]] on the bus and then speaks to them at the table. One of them corrects her [[gently]], and she tries again. The caption asks, “Who would you like to speak to?” A green download button and the trial [[length]] appear below. The comments include learners [[sharing]] names of people they hope to visit.

title: Gaming headphones
text: Before a cinema screening, a gaming-headphone advert starts with a team losing an online match because they cannot hear a [[warning]]. The screen [[splits]] to show the players in different homes, including a girl who [[leads]] the next plan. With the new headphones, each voice is clear, and they finish the game together. The slogan says, “Hear everyone on your side.” The final shot shows the [[microphone]], product price and shop website.

title: Premium noise-cancelling headphones
text: A radio advert for premium noise-cancelling headphones begins with crowded café sounds. A woman tells her friend she needs to finish writing a song before her train leaves. After she puts on the headphones, we hear the [[melody]] she is building [[rather]] than the room. She takes them off to [[answer]] her friend. The narrator explains that listeners can [[control]] which sounds come through, then names the model and its premium price.

title: Family tablet
text: In this television advert for a family tablet, three [[siblings]] share the screen on a rainy afternoon. One draws a dragon, another reads aloud, and the oldest helps their grandmother join a video call. Their parents appear [[briefly]] in the kitchen but do not direct every activity. A final shot shows the tablet [[propped]] up for a family recipe. The voiceover calls it “a screen for doing things together,” and the price appears beside a short [[warranty]] notice.

title: Professional camera
text: A website banner for a professional camera shows two [[portraits]] of the same street vendor. In one, he is a blurred figure behind his stall; in the other, his face and hands are [[sharply]] focused. The photographer, a young woman, appears in a small reflection rather than the main frame. Text reads, “See the person in the picture.” A clickable panel opens [[specifications]] and sample images, while a caption identifies the vendor by name with his [[permission]].

title: Fitness tracker
text: This podcast advert for a fitness tracker is recorded as a conversation between a runner and her father. She describes training for a race; he describes walking every evening after [[recovering]] from an illness. Both check their [[progress]] on the same device, but [[neither]] mentions losing weight. Their different [[goals]] make exercise seem possible at more than one age or level of fitness. The host gives the price and says the tracker can be used without a paid coaching plan.

title: Home security system
text: In a radio advert for a home security system, a woman hears her front gate open while she is working late. Her phone tells her that her teenage son has arrived home, and she asks if he wants dinner. The scene is calm rather than frightening. A voiceover explains the camera alert and door [[sensor]] before saying, “Know when your people are home.” The advert presents security as everyday [[reassurance]], then gives a website and a [[monthly]] [[subscription]] price.

title: Entry-level laptop
text: A website banner for an entry-level laptop is divided into three moving pictures. A student edits a school project, a mechanic checks a repair [[manual]], and an older man writes to his sister. Each person uses the same model in a different place. The line “Ready for your next task” appears over a clearly [[displayed]] starting price. When visitors tap the banner, they see the laptop's storage, battery life and [[accessibility]] settings [[rather]] than a picture of an expensive office.

title: Family car
text: This television advert for a family car opens with a father trying to fit a large cake into the [[boot]]. His daughter offers a better way to arrange the bags, while her mother checks the [[route]] from the passenger seat. They arrive at a crowded birthday party with the cake [[intact]]. The car's space is [[demonstrated]] through a small problem rather than a list of numbers. A price and safety rating appear on screen after the family goes inside.

title: Luxury car
text: A luxury car advert on television follows a woman driving through a city before dawn. She stops to collect her elderly father, who quietly admires the comfortable seat. No one mistakes her for a [[chauffeur]] or congratulates her for owning the car. The camera [[lingers]] on the [[interior]], then widens to show a busy morning street. “Make room for what matters,” says the voiceover. The brand name appears at the end, with no price or finance [[offer]].

title: City bicycle
text: A sponsored social post for a city bicycle follows a nurse leaving work at sunset. She rides along a marked cycle [[lane]], stops for [[groceries]] and reaches home before the rain. The caption says, “A different way across town,” and lists the bike's lights and carrying basket. The nurse is shown as tired but [[capable]], and the city has ordinary traffic rather than empty streets. A second image gives the price, [[sizing]] guide and nearby shops.

title: Racing bicycle
text: In a social post for a racing bicycle, a cyclist finishes a difficult climb and waits at the top for the rest of her club. The photos include riders of different ages, though the lightest and most expensive bike is hers. The caption describes the frame's [[weight]] and a race result, then invites readers to explore the [[specifications]]. The group photograph keeps the focus on shared training [[instead]] of presenting success as something achieved [[entirely]] alone.

title: Budget hotel stay
text: A podcast advert for a budget hotel stay begins with the sound of keys, luggage wheels and a kettle. Two friends describe returning from a concert and making tea in their clean, small room. They joke about the view of a car park but praise the late check-in and helpful [[receptionist]]. A narrator gives the [[nightly]] price and booking [[conditions]]. The advert treats an affordable trip as enjoyable without [[pretending]] that the room is luxurious.

title: Luxury hotel stay
text: This magazine advert for a luxury hotel shows a woman reading on a shaded [[balcony]] above the sea. Through the open door, a staff member places flowers on a table, but their face is not visible.
