The headline says, “Everything taken care of.” Gold [[lettering]] and a full-page photograph create a calm, expensive mood. A small note mentions private [[transfers]] and a personal host. The picture suggests comfort, while giving almost no attention to the people who [[provide]] it.

title: Household vacuum cleaner
text: A social post for a household vacuum cleaner begins with a father dropping a bowl of cereal just before guests arrive. His daughter fetches the vacuum and shows him which [[attachment]] reaches the corners. Both laugh as they clean. The caption lists the price and the machine's weight, with a link to a short [[demonstration]]. The advert presents housework as a shared family task and gives the child practical [[knowledge]] rather than making her a helpless [[onlooker]].

title: Premium robot vacuum
text: In a magazine advert for a premium robot vacuum, an architect comes home to a tidy apartment and puts her feet up with a book. The device crosses the floor in the lower corner of the picture. Text says, “One less job on your list,” and a [[diagram]] shows how it avoids [[furniture]]. Her home is spacious and almost empty, making the product seem [[effortless]] to use. The small print gives a high price and notes that some [[features]] need an app.

title: Flat-pack sofa
text: A website banner for a flat-pack sofa shows a family carrying three boxes up a narrow [[staircase]]. In the next moving image, two adults and a teenager fit the pieces together while a younger child sorts the [[screws]]. The line “Bring it home yourself” sits above a price and a link to [[assembly]] instructions. The room is a modest rented flat, with books on the floor. The advert makes limited space part of the story instead of [[hiding]] it.

title: Designer sofa
text: In a podcast advert for a designer sofa, an interior designer describes visiting an older couple whose living room has held decades of family gatherings. They choose a new sofa together, discussing the [[fabric]] and seat height as carefully as its appearance. Soft conversation and a closing door create the scene through sound. The host names the collection and offers a [[consultation]] link, but gives no price. The couple are presented as people with [[taste]], not as grandparents waiting in the [[background]].

title: Shampoo
text: A cinema advert for shampoo opens on a huge close-up of wet hair, then pulls back to [[reveal]] a teenager preparing for a school concert. Her friend, who has short hair, helps her fix the [[microphone]] rather than commenting on her appearance. As the band begins, the [[soundtrack]] grows louder and the product name appears beside a simple claim about gentle washing. The story links confidence to [[performing]] with friends; the shampoo remains a small part of getting ready.

title: Premium skincare serum
text: An online video for a premium skincare serum follows a woman in her fifties through a morning at her [[pottery]] studio. She washes [[clay]] from her hands, [[applies]] the serum and returns to her wheel. The camera shows the lines around her eyes clearly, without a before-and-after comparison. A caption explains the ingredients and their stated purpose, while a link gives the price. She is represented through her craft as well as her skin, and her age is [[neither]] hidden nor treated as a problem.

title: Mobile data plan
text: A podcast advert for a mobile data plan uses short voice messages between three relatives. A teenager sends a photograph from a school trip, her uncle replies from a train, and their grandmother records a message from home. The narrator explains the shared-data [[allowance]] and what happens when it runs out. The voices make the plan seem useful across [[generations]], while the clear limit and monthly price keep the offer [[understandable]]. The grandmother contributes the funniest line in the [[exchange]].

title: Private tutoring service
text: A transit poster for a private tutoring service shows a boy and his tutor working through a maths problem at a kitchen table. The boy has [[crossed]] out several answers, and the tutor points to one useful step rather than [[completing]] the work for him. The headline reads, “Confidence grows with practice.” A QR code leads to tutor [[profiles]] and prices. His school uniform and neat home suggest a particular kind of family, even [[though]] the wording promises help for any learner.

title: Gym membership
text: This transit poster for a gym [[membership]] shows three members leaving a class together: a young man carrying a sports bag, a middle-aged woman using a walking stick, and an older man in running shoes. “Start where you are,” says the headline. The poster gives opening hours, an [[introductory]] price and a map of the nearest [[branch]]. None of the people has a dramatic transformation photograph. Their different bodies make [[participation]] the main promise rather than a particular shape.

title: Wellness retreat
text: In an online video for a wellness retreat, a teacher arrives looking [[exhausted]] and switches off her phone. Over three days she walks, joins a group meal and spends time alone by a lake. The voiceover offers “space to think” instead of promising a [[cure]]. Other guests appear briefly, but staff preparing meals and leading activities remain mostly out of [[frame]]. A final card shows the location, dates and a [[substantial]] starting price, making the invitation clearly exclusive.

title: Children’s board game
text: A magazine advert for a children's board game shows two cousins and their grandfather arguing cheerfully over the [[rules]]. The youngest child notices a move that everyone else [[missed]]. Colourful pieces cover the table, and the headline says, “Everyone gets a turn to surprise you.” A short box explains the age [[range]] and playing time. The photograph presents the grandfather as a player who can lose, while the children are shown thinking rather than [[merely]] smiling for adults.

title: Collectable toy set
text: A transit poster for a collectable toy set places three detailed figures against a dramatic night sky. One wears a cape, another has [[mechanical]] wings, and the third uses a wheelchair built into a futuristic vehicle. “Build your own team” appears above a QR code linking to the full range. The small text gives the price and says the figures are sold [[separately]]. The characters are presented as [[equally]] capable, although completing the advertised scene would cost [[considerably]] more.

title: Streaming subscription
text: A website banner for a streaming subscription changes as the visitor moves over it. A grandmother watches a mystery, two teenagers choose a comedy, and a young man watches a cooking programme with [[subtitles]]. The line “Find your next story” remains in the centre. A button opens the [[catalogue]] and a clearly stated monthly price. The different viewers suggest a [[broad]] audience, while the small print explains that some live events require an [[additional]] payment.

title: Premium bank account
text: This magazine advert for a premium bank account shows a woman standing at an airport window, looking over a city at night. Her suitcase and business papers suggest [[frequent]] travel, but the advert never states her job. The headline reads, “Wherever work takes you.” A smaller panel lists travel support, lounge [[access]] and the monthly fee. The image presents her as [[independent]] and successful, while the benefits and setting imply that this version of success requires considerable [[income]].

title: Orange juice
text: Before a cinema screening, an orange juice advert fills the screen with a family kitchen at dawn. A grandfather cuts fruit while his granddaughter prepares breakfast for everyone else; the parents hurry in from their night shifts. As the juice is poured, the pale room turns warm and bright. The line “Start together, whenever your day begins” [[acknowledges]] that not every family keeps [[conventional]] hours. The carton and a promotional price appear only at the end, alongside small print about its sugar content. No single parent is assigned the task of [[feeding]] the [[household]].

title: Cold-pressed juice
text: A website banner for cold-pressed juice shows a chef finishing work in a spotless restaurant kitchen. She opens a glass bottle and takes a break beside another chef, whose [[apron]] is stained from service. A moving close-up highlights the liquid's colour and the [[ingredients]] listed on its label. The line “Made for the hours you put in” connects an expensive drink with professional [[effort]] rather than effortless wellness. A button reveals the price and delivery area. The kitchen workers have names in the caption, [[although]] the cleaners who appear in the background do not.

title: Breakfast cereal
text: This transit poster for breakfast cereal depicts a father and son waiting for an early bus, each holding a bowl with a secure [[lid]]. Their school and work bags sit between them. A small drawing explains the cereal's [[wholegrain]] ingredients, while the headline says, “Breakfast travels with you.” The boy is pointing out a bird on the pavement; his father listens rather than staring at his phone. The poster treats their journey as ordinary family time. The colourful packaging and a supermarket price [[occupy]] the lower corner, where [[commuters]] can read them quickly.

title: Boxed chocolates
text: In a magazine advert for boxed chocolates, an older woman opens the door to find her adult daughter standing there [[unexpectedly]]. They share the chocolates over tea while a family photograph remains partly visible behind them. The photograph and warm indoor light suggest a long [[relationship]] without explaining why the daughter has returned. “Some visits deserve a proper pause” appears beneath the box. The image presents the gift as a way to begin a conversation, not a [[replacement]] for one. The premium price is [[absent]], although the shop address and handmade claim are printed below.

title: Instant noodles
text: A cinema advert for instant noodles begins with the imposing soundtrack of an action film. A student [[strides]] through a dark corridor towards a glowing kitchen, only for the camera to [[reveal]] that her dramatic mission is to prepare a late supper. Her flatmate joins her, and the [[heroic]] music gives way to their laughter. A close-up shows the packet, cooking time and price. The joke gives both young women control of the story rather than using them as [[decoration]]. The final slogan, “Big night, small budget,” makes the ordinary meal feel playful.

title: Meal kit
text: A radio advert for a meal kit plays the sound of a front door opening, followed by a quick [[exchange]] between two housemates. One has brought home the ingredients; the other reads the instructions aloud and admits that he has never cooked the dish. We hear chopping, a small mistake and finally plates being set down. A narrator explains the [[subscription]] price and how to skip a week. Their conversation makes cooking sound [[learnable]] and shared, while the [[absence]] of an expert chef avoids suggesting that only confident cooks can use the service.

title: Supermarket coffee
text: This television advert for supermarket coffee follows a city bus driver through a winter morning. At the [[depot]], she pours coffee into a [[flask]] and offers another cup to a colleague who has just finished his shift. Outside, the city slowly wakes. The brand appears on the familiar supermarket packet beside a modest price. “For the starts nobody sees” is spoken over a shot of the driver greeting her first passengers. The advert gives [[dignity]] to routine work, although its warm portrait of early shifts leaves little room for their physical [[strain]].

title: Speciality coffee
text: A billboard for speciality coffee shows two farmers standing beside coffee plants after rain. Their names and the region appear in large type, while the roaster's brand is smaller. The line “Know [[whose]] morning begins yours” sits above a drawing of the beans' journey to the café. At street level, a QR code links to a longer account and the premium price. The image gives the [[growers]] a visible identity, but the single photograph cannot show how the price is [[divided]] among everyone involved in [[production]].

title: Sports drink
text: On a billboard for a sports drink, a teenage goalkeeper has just made a save in a muddy local match. Teammates run towards her, while a boy on the [[opposing]] side gets up and smiles despite the missed goal. The slogan, “Ready for the next minute,” is printed beside the bottle. Rather than using a stadium or celebrity athlete, the advert places sporting [[achievement]] on an ordinary public pitch. A small [[nutrition]] panel sits at the bottom, but drivers passing quickly may notice the [[triumphant]] image long before the drink's ingredients.

title: Bottled water
text: A radio advert for bottled water opens with the sounds of a crowded train and a child asking for a drink. Her father offers a [[refillable]] bottle, then notices that it is empty. At the next stop they buy water, and he promises to refill the bottle when they get home. The narrator gives the price and describes the cap's [[recycled]] material. This small, slightly awkward story presents bottled water as useful on [[occasion]] rather than an essential daily purchase. The child is allowed to question her father's [[forgetfulness]].

title: Everyday watch
text: In this radio advert for an everyday watch, a man misses the time because his phone battery has died during a school sports day. His daughter, who is competing, calls out the minutes before her race begins. Later, he [[fastens]] a simple watch around his [[wrist]]. The ticking sound becomes part of the closing music, followed by a clear price and shop name. The story presents fatherhood through attention and [[reliability]], while the daughter remains the athlete [[whose]] event gives the watch its meaning.

title: Luxury watch
text: A cinema advert for a luxury watch shows a female conductor preparing an orchestra. The [[auditorium]] is empty as she raises her hand, and a close-up reveals the watch beneath her sleeve. Sound drops away for a second before the musicians begin together. “Time belongs to the person who makes the moment” appears against black. The campaign gives an older woman [[authority]] and professional skill, rather than showing her as someone's partner. The instrument makers and musicians remain mostly [[anonymous]], while the final gold logo and absence of a price signal [[exclusivity]].

title: School trainers
text: A sponsored social post for school trainers features four pupils preparing for different parts of their day: a walk to school, a basketball game, a dance rehearsal and the journey home. A [[carousel]] lets viewers swipe between worn [[soles]] and clean new shoes. The caption gives a price, available sizes and a link to a repair [[scheme]]. Each child names something they enjoy doing, so the shoes support [[distinct]] personalities rather than creating one ideal kind of pupil. A visible “Ad” label sits above the first photograph.

title: Designer trainers
text: A website banner for designer trainers presents a young violinist walking across a city in formal concert clothes and brightly coloured shoes. As she moves, the banner briefly freezes on details of the stitching and sole. The headline reads, “No uniform for [[ambition]].” A link opens an interview about her work, followed by product photographs and a high price. Her skill offers a more specific identity than the usual street-style pose, although the expensive shoes are framed as an [[expression]] of [[independence]] that many viewers cannot [[afford]].

title: Waterproof coat
text: A website banner for a waterproof coat shows a woman and her teenage nephew waiting at a rainy football pitch. She coaches his team, and he holds her [[clipboard]] while she demonstrates where the players should stand. Raindrops run off her coat beneath the words “Stay for the whole game.” A clickable lower strip reveals the price, size range and waterproof [[rating]]. The advert avoids presenting outdoor activity as a test of [[toughness]]; the coach is there for the children, and the coat makes staying [[comfortable]] possible.

title: Designer coat
text: In a sponsored social post for a designer coat, an architect stands on an unfinished building's roof, examining her drawings against the [[skyline]]. The long coat moves in the wind, contrasting with the practical boots beneath it. The caption names the design house and describes the [[fabric]], while the “Ad” label and shop link are clearly visible. She is [[represented]] as someone whose decisions shape the city, though the campaign uses her workplace mainly as a striking background. [[Construction]] workers appear in one wide shot without being named.

title: Basic handbag
text: A cinema advert for a basic handbag follows a mother teaching her son to travel across town alone. She packs a map, snacks and her own keys into a [[sturdy]] bag, then lets him carry his ticket and choose the right bus. When they reach his [[destination]], he walks ahead confidently. The bag's [[compartments]] are shown through the action, and the final card gives a price. The story recognises the mother's care but also shows her gradually handing [[responsibility]] to the child rather than holding him back.

title: Designer handbag
text: In an online video for a designer handbag, a young museum [[curator]] prepares an exhibition opening. She carries handwritten notes and a small repair kit in the bag as she checks the display. Guests arrive, and the camera shifts from her [[anxious]] expression to the work she has organised. The caption links to the handbag and lists its [[materials]] without showing a price until the viewer clicks. The advert presents professional [[achievement]] as attractive, yet its close-ups repeatedly return from the exhibition to the expensive object on her arm.

title: Everyday fragrance
text: This television advert for everyday fragrance follows a university student visiting his grandmother before an important interview. She recognises the [[scent]] and tells him that his grandfather used to wear something similar, then helps him straighten his [[collar]]. In the next scene he enters the interview room, where a woman leads the panel. The slogan reads, “A little courage goes with you.” Packaging and a supermarket price close the advert. The fragrance is tied to memory and [[reassurance]] rather than a promise that wearing it will [[guarantee]] success.

title: Luxury perfume
text: A radio advert for luxury perfume begins with a woman describing an empty theatre from the stage. We hear her footsteps, a curtain moving and the distant sound of an audience arriving. She says the scent reminds her of the first performance she [[directed]], when she finally trusted her own decisions. A low voice names the perfume and a department store, but offers no ingredients or price. The advert gives her a [[creative]] history; [[listeners]] must imagine both her [[appearance]] and the expensive bottle being sold.

title: Budget smartphone
text: This transit poster for a budget smartphone shows a cleaner calling her daughter after an evening shift. The daughter is sitting at a desk with a map of the city, helping plan tomorrow's [[route]]. The headline promises “The conversations that matter, at a price that works.” A large [[figure]] gives the phone's starting cost, with storage and contract details underneath. The mother is [[represented]] as an active parent managing time and money. The poster's emotional scene is supported by practical information that passing [[commuters]] can check.

title: Flagship smartphone
text: In a television advert for a flagship smartphone, a young documentary maker films her neighbourhood's [[annual]] street festival. She records a drummer, an older baker and children making [[decorations]], then shows the finished short film at an outdoor gathering. Fast cuts demonstrate the camera's low-light performance, while a title card names the feature. “Every place has a story worth keeping” closes the advert. The expensive handset is associated with a community's [[visibility]], although the story depends on one person [[owning]] the latest technology.

title: Language-learning app
text: A billboard for a language-learning app depicts a woman ordering food in two [[overlapping]] photographs. In the first she points at the menu, while in the second she laughs with the waiter and speaks a short sentence printed in a speech bubble. The headline asks, “What could you say next month?” A QR code offers a trial and a line below explains the [[subscription]] price afterwards. The woman is neither mocked for making mistakes nor [[transformed]] into a perfect speaker; the change is presented as increased [[willingness]] to try.

title: Gaming headphones
text: Before a cinema screening, an advert for gaming headphones opens with a player hearing a teammate's quiet warning behind the film's booming soundtrack. A split screen shows four friends in separate rooms, including a boy using a wheelchair who directs their [[strategy]]. Their voices become clearer as the game unfolds, and the final victory is [[collective]]. The product's microphone and surround-sound [[settings]] appear beside the price. The campaign presents the disabled player as a decision maker within the group, not as an inspirational [[exception]].

title: Premium noise-cancelling headphones
text: A transit poster for premium noise-cancelling headphones shows a woman sitting in a busy station with a notebook open on her lap. The crowd around her is [[rendered]] as blurred [[streaks]], but a friend beside her remains sharply visible. “Choose what comes through” appears above a small explanation of the listening modes. A QR code leads to a demonstration and the high price. The composition suggests that concentration need not mean [[withdrawing]] from people altogether, while the spotless headphones stand out against the station's untidy [[realism]].

title: Family tablet
text: An online video for a family tablet begins with a grandmother teaching two children a card game. When the rules become complicated, the older child records her [[explanation]] on the tablet; later, they use it to call a cousin who lives [[abroad]]. The screen remains visible without replacing the cards or the conversation. “Keep the good bits going” appears beside the model and price. The grandmother supplies the knowledge, while the children help with the technology, so [[expertise]] moves in both directions across the [[generations]].

title: Professional camera
text: In an online video for a professional camera, a photographer takes portraits of workers at a night market. He asks a cook's [[permission]] before photographing her, then shows her the image on the camera screen. The cook suggests a different [[angle]] that includes the whole stall. Close-ups demonstrate the camera's controls in low light; a final card links to technical [[specifications]] and the premium price. The small exchange gives the person being photographed some [[authority]] over how she is represented, rather than treating her simply as an interesting face.

title: Fitness tracker
text: This television advert for a fitness tracker follows three people through an ordinary Tuesday. A delivery rider checks the distance [[travelled]], an office worker takes a short walk at lunch, and an older woman records a gentle exercise class. Their numbers differ, and none is described as a winner. The voiceover says, “Measure your day on your terms,” while the screen shows the tracker and its health settings. The closing price includes a note about [[optional]] paid features. The advert values varied [[routines]], though every activity is still [[converted]] into data.

title: Home security system
text: A sponsored social post for a home security system shows a couple returning from a weekend away. Their door camera has recorded a neighbour watering the plants and a parcel being left safely. The caption explains how [[alerts]] can be shared with trusted people, while a short clip shows one partner setting the system up. Both [[participate]] in the decisions. A clearly marked “Ad” label, [[installation]] cost and monthly fee appear [[beneath]] the video. The story sells a sense of community as well as technology, despite depending on constant recording.

title: Entry-level laptop
text: A billboard for an entry-level laptop shows a young man at a library table, helping his mother complete an online course. Beside them, another student uses the same model to edit a presentation. “Good work starts somewhere” sits above the price in unusually large type. A QR code leads to a list of the laptop's [[specifications]] and repair options. The advert makes adult learning visible and treats the son as a [[collaborator]] rather than a digital rescuer. The public library setting gives the affordable device a [[credible]] everyday [[context]].

title: Family car
text: In a sponsored social post for a family car, a parent describes the weekly journey between two homes after a [[separation]]. The video shows a father collecting his daughter, making space for her music case and asking which [[route]] she prefers. The mother waves from the door; she is part of the family without being inside the car. A caption lists the vehicle's safety features, price and finance terms. The small story [[broadens]] the usual image of family travel, while the sponsor label keeps its [[commercial]] purpose visible.

title: Luxury car
text: A transit poster for a luxury car shows a sharply dressed woman seated in the back, revising notes before a public speech. The driver is visible only through a [[reflection]] in the window. “Arrive ready” appears beside the car's name in silver lettering; neither a price nor a practical [[specification]] is provided. Her professional responsibility makes her more than a passive passenger, but the blurred driver illustrates whose [[labour]] the image chooses to overlook. The poster invites commuters to identify with the calm, [[privileged]] person being transported.

title: City bicycle
text: This magazine advert for a city bicycle shows an older man cycling past shops that have known him for decades. He stops to collect bread, checks his lights and greets a young neighbour riding to school. The headline, “Your city is still yours,” sits above a map of local cycle [[routes]]. A smaller panel gives the bike's price, weight and step-through [[frame]] details. His age is presented through his [[relationships]] and knowledge of the neighbourhood rather than through a [[claim]] that the bicycle will make him feel young again.

title: Racing bicycle
text: An online video for a racing bicycle follows a woman returning to training after an [[injury]]. She adjusts the bike with her coach, rides a short stretch and stops when her leg begins to hurt. Later scenes show gradual improvement, not an instant race victory. Technical captions explain the frame's fit and weight, followed by its high price. Her decisions about [[recovery]] carry the story; the bike supports her work without pretending to remove its [[difficulty]]. The coach is credited on [[screen]], an unusual detail in a performance-focused campaign.

title: Budget hotel stay
text: A billboard for a budget hotel stay shows two friends eating takeaway food on the bed after a day exploring a new city. Their shoes and maps are [[scattered]] around a small but tidy room. “Save on the room. Stay for the trip” appears beside the [[nightly]] price. The hotel name, location and booking QR code are easy to read from a bus stop. The image treats a limited budget as a [[sensible]] travel choice, although it shows none of the staff who clean and [[prepare]] the room.

title: Luxury hotel stay
text: In a podcast advert for a luxury hotel, a travel writer describes waking before sunrise to hear the harbour. A [[concierge]] then speaks about arranging a boat trip, and a chef explains one breakfast dish. Their names are given, but the writer receives the longest speaking time. Soft music and the sound of waves create a private, unhurried atmosphere. The host names the hotel's [[suites]] and booking link without stating a price. The advert makes service [[central]] to the experience while carefully [[controlling]] how much the workers can say.

title: Household vacuum cleaner
text: An online video for a household vacuum cleaner shows a shared apartment preparing for a party. Three flatmates [[divide]] the jobs: one tidies books, another cooks, and the third uses the vacuum on a rug. When a guest arrives early, they finish together. A product close-up shows the [[attachments]], and a caption gives the price and [[warranty]]. None of the flatmates is made the permanent cleaner. The advert presents a [[functional]] machine within an imperfect home, where tidiness is something people create together before welcoming friends.

title: Premium robot vacuum
text: In a podcast advert for a premium robot vacuum, a novelist describes the noise of her apartment settling after her children leave for school. She starts the vacuum through an app, then reads her [[draft]] aloud while it works. Her partner calls to ask about dinner, and they agree to share the cooking. The host explains [[scheduling]], the high price and [[maintenance]] needs. The story sells an extra hour for creative work, although the machine can only perform one part of the household [[labour]] that usually interrupts it.

title: Flat-pack sofa
text: A website banner for a flat-pack sofa presents a [[sequence]] of photographs taken in the same small living room. Two friends [[assemble]] the sofa, a neighbour helps carry away the boxes, and a child later turns the cushions into a fort. “Made for life after the instructions” appears above the price and delivery options. Clicking opens a [[genuine]] assembly guide. The people and room are slightly untidy, giving the furniture a lived-in setting. The neighbour is more than a convenient extra pair of hands: she joins the final [[gathering]].

title: Designer sofa
text: A podcast advert for a designer sofa is built around a conversation between a furniture maker and a woman choosing a seat for her mother. They discuss fabric, support and how her mother likes to read by the window. The mother then joins the conversation and firmly rejects the first colour. The maker explains the materials, followed by a [[consultation]] link and no stated price. Her voice [[prevents]] the older woman from becoming merely a reason for someone else's purchase, while the [[bespoke]] service signals a wealthy [[audience]].

title: Shampoo
text: In a podcast advert for shampoo, a teenage swimmer describes the smell of the pool and the long journey home after training. Her father asks about her race while she washes her hair; she talks more about her teammates than her time. A narrator briefly names the shampoo's gentle formula, price and shop availability. Splashes and [[muffled]] conversation make the scene vivid without requiring any [[visual]] promise of perfect hair. The swimmer's sport and friendships define her, while the product [[occupies]] a practical moment in her [[routine]].

title: Premium skincare serum
text: A sponsored social post for premium skincare serum features a woman in her sixties explaining how she cares for her skin before working outdoors in her garden. She names the serum, then reminds viewers that she also wears a hat and [[sunscreen]]. The caption lists the ingredients, price and sponsored [[partnership]]. Natural light leaves wrinkles visible, and her gardening knowledge fills more of the video than the product demonstration. The campaign offers an expensive routine without [[implying]] that age itself is a [[flaw]] to be corrected.

title: Mobile data plan
text: This transit poster for a mobile data plan depicts two brothers exchanging photographs of a family celebration. One is travelling by train; the other is helping their father set up the tables at home. The headline says, “Still in the room,” beside a plainly stated monthly [[allowance]] and price. Small print explains the speed after the allowance is used. The family appears connected across [[distance]], although the poster's central image of the smiling traveller makes the brother doing the practical preparation less [[noticeable]] at first [[glance]].

title: Private tutoring service
text: A magazine advert for private tutoring shows a girl correcting her own essay with a tutor sitting beside her. Several [[drafts]] are spread over the table, and a handwritten note says, “This sentence says what I mean.” The headline, “The answer should sound like you,” links tutoring with confidence rather than a guaranteed grade. [[Qualifications]], session format and a high hourly rate appear in a side panel. The girl's [[revision]] work is visible, but the calm private study and price also reveal which families can most [[readily]] purchase this help.

title: Gym membership
text: This television advert for a gym membership opens with a crowded beginner's class in which the instructor demonstrates easier and harder versions of the same movement. [[Participants]] choose their own [[pace]], including a young man who pauses and an older woman who continues. The music fades as the instructor says, “You can come back tomorrow.” The final screen lists facilities, access information and the monthly price. The advert presents fitness as repeated [[participation]] rather than a dramatic [[transformation]], although the camera still favours the most energetic members.

title: Wellness retreat
text: In a magazine advert for a wellness retreat, two friends sit silently on a path above a forest. One wears walking boots, while the other holds a sketchbook; neither is posed in a yoga position. “A little room around your thoughts” is printed below the photograph. A separate panel names the programme, [[duration]] and substantial price. The peaceful scene gives the women individual interests, but the retreat's brochure also describes meals and guided activities without [[depicting]] the people who provide them. [[Solitude]] is represented as something carefully [[organised]] for paying guests.

title: Children’s board game
text: A podcast advert for a children's board game begins with an argument about [[whose]] turn it is. A girl reads the rules, her uncle admits he misunderstood them, and a younger boy solves the puzzle that follows. Their laughter is interrupted by the satisfying [[clatter]] of game pieces. The narrator gives the age range, playing time and price. Adults are [[fallible]] players rather than judges, while the children take different [[intellectual]] roles. The advert promises time spent together without pretending that family games are always perfectly peaceful.

title: Collectable toy set
text: A radio advert for a collectable toy set uses a [[miniature]] adventure told entirely through sound. One character hears a door closing, another designs a bridge, and a third drives the team to safety. The closing [[narrator]] identifies all three figures and explains that they are sold separately, with their individual prices. Their different voices and tasks make the characters [[distinct]] without relying on appearance. The imaginative story, however, suggests that a complete adventure may require [[purchasing]] more than the first figure.

title: Streaming subscription
text: This magazine advert for a streaming subscription arranges six small photographs like frames from different stories. A teenager watches a nature series with [[subtitles]], a couple share a comedy, and a retired woman chooses a crime drama alone. “Your night, your story” appears above the monthly price and a trial offer. The range of viewers suggests that being alone is not a problem the service must fix. A [[footnote]] [[clarifies]] the trial's end date and explains that the cheapest plan [[includes]] adverts.

title: Premium bank account
text: A website banner for a premium bank account depicts a woman checking an account on her phone before entering a meeting. Its moving background changes from an airport to a quiet office, suggesting that her financial life crosses borders. The words “More control, wherever you work” lead to a page of travel benefits, fees and [[eligibility]] rules. She is clearly the account [[holder]] and decision maker. The elegant settings and [[selective]] entry conditions also connect financial [[competence]] with a particular level of professional success.

title: Orange juice
text: A sponsored social post for orange juice opens with a mother packing breakfast while her partner wakes their children. The camera then moves to their neighbour, an older man who joins them at the table with a newspaper and a homemade [[loaf]]. The caption reads, “However your morning begins, make room for someone.” A recipe link and a clearly marked promotional price sit below the video. The family is presented as a [[network]] of care extending beyond the household, although the neighbour's arrival [[conveniently]] leaves the crowded kitchen looking spacious and cheerful. A [[nutrition]] panel appears only when viewers open the product details.

title: Cold-pressed juice
text: In an online video for cold-pressed juice, a designer describes the intense preparations for her first [[exhibition]]. Between scenes of arranging furniture and correcting labels, she drinks the juice with the security guard who has watched the space take shape. The film briefly gives him a name before returning to her voiceover. “For the days you build something” appears beside the glass bottle, ingredient list and premium price. The campaign lends the drink an [[association]] with creative labour, while the guard's presence acknowledges, then quickly moves past, another kind of work [[essential]] to the event. A paid-partnership notice remains visible [[throughout]].

title: Breakfast cereal
text: This sponsored social post for breakfast cereal is filmed by a father during a chaotic morning with his three children. The youngest insists on [[pouring]] her own milk; the oldest checks the bus time; their sister makes lunch while refusing help. Nothing goes entirely smoothly, and the final caption says, “There is no perfect breakfast.” The cereal box, supermarket offer and a short ingredient list appear in the last frame. By letting the children disagree and make choices, the advert resists the picture of a silent, [[grateful]] family, although its carefully [[edited]] [[disorder]] still leads to an unusually tidy ending.

title: Boxed chocolates
text: A social post for boxed chocolates follows two sisters visiting their mother in a care home. One brings flowers, while the other brings the chocolates and remembers which [[flavour]] their mother dislikes. The three spend most of the short video talking about an old photograph rather than opening the box. The caption, “A gift can start the visit,” links to the premium range, and a sponsored label is clearly displayed. Their mother speaks for herself and teases her daughters, giving her more [[presence]] than the setting might initially suggest. The campaign [[nevertheless]] turns a complex family visit into a polished moment of [[consumer]] warmth.

title: Instant noodles
text: A podcast advert for instant noodles is framed as a conversation between flatmates after a long shift. One describes a difficult customer; the other has left the kettle on and asks [[whether]] they should share the last packet. Their voices overlap, and the preparation sounds continue beneath a short narrator's message giving the cooking time and low price. “Not every dinner needs a plan” closes the segment. The advert locates comfort in [[companionship]] rather than [[culinary]] skill, but its relaxed account of late work offers no explanation for the [[precarious]] hours that brought both people home exhausted.

title: Meal kit
text: Before a cinema feature, a meal-kit advert shows an adult son attempting to cook his mother's favourite dish for her birthday. She arrives early, notices his mistake and teaches him how to correct it, while his husband [[lays]] the table. The camera follows the exchange more closely than the recipe steps. Only after dinner does the kit appear beside its weekly cost and a reminder that [[subscriptions]] can be paused. “Good meals leave room for someone else's method” is the closing line. The mother retains her [[expertise]], even as the packaged ingredients quietly position a paid service inside a family [[tradition]].

title: Supermarket coffee
text: A cinema advert for supermarket coffee opens on the empty stage of a community theatre. A cleaner finishes her work, pours coffee from a flask and pauses to watch a young actor [[rehearsing]] alone. When he loses his place, she supplies the next line: she knows the entire play. The closing card shows the packet and modest price beneath “There is more to everyone you pass.” By granting her knowledge and [[agency]], the film interrupts an easy [[assumption]] about invisible labour. Its uplifting reveal, however, resolves the question of how she is valued through a brief moment of [[recognition]].

title: Speciality coffee
text: In a podcast advert for speciality coffee, a café owner calls a grower to discuss the coming [[harvest]]. We hear both sides of the conversation, including the grower's explanation that heavy rain has reduced this year's crop. The owner then describes a higher purchase price and the flavour customers can expect. A link offers [[sourcing]] details and the premium [[retail]] price. “A good cup has a longer story” concludes the segment. The grower is represented as an expert making decisions, although the café still controls the final account presented to listeners and the claims available for them to [[verify]].

title: Sports drink
text: A cinema advert for a sports drink begins with a [[relay]] team losing a race by a narrow margin. Instead of cutting directly to a rematch, it shows an athlete with a [[prosthetic]] leg discussing the handover with a teammate, and another runner admitting that he started too quickly. Training scenes follow, then a second race ends before the result is revealed. The slogan, “There is always another lap,” appears beside the bottle and a short nutrition [[disclosure]]. The athletes are given specific tactical roles, while the [[unresolved]] ending avoids reducing the disabled runner to a simple story of exceptional triumph.

title: Bottled water
text: A magazine advert for bottled water places a clear bottle beside a public drinking fountain, where a woman is [[refilling]] her own container. The headline asks, “When you need another option.” Smaller text identifies the bottle's size, price and recycled content, without claiming that buying one is an environmental solution. The woman is dressed for work and holds a child's coat; the photograph offers [[fragments]] of her day without making her a symbol of motherhood. The unusual placement of the fountain admits the existence of a cheaper [[alternative]], even as the composition keeps the branded bottle sharply lit in the [[foreground]].

title: Everyday watch
text: This radio advert for an everyday watch begins with a young nurse describing how the minutes between patient checks can feel different from the minutes on her journey home. Colleagues call her by name, and a patient asks when his daughter will arrive. A quiet ticking sound [[bridges]] the scenes. The narrator gives a practical price, water-resistance information and a shop address, then says, “Keep time where it helps.” Her professional attention lends the watch [[significance]], although the compressed story cannot [[convey]] the wider conditions under which that attention must be [[sustained]].

title: Luxury watch
text: A website banner for a luxury watch shows a celebrated architect examining a half-built public library. When viewers move the [[cursor]], the image shifts from her wrist to a drawing of the finished building; a third panel briefly includes the construction crew. “For what remains after you leave” appears beside the watch's name, with no price. Her [[authorship]] and age are visible in a campaign that could easily have chosen a younger model. Yet the banner grants the crew only a passing appearance, making [[collective]] construction serve a story about one individual's lasting [[legacy]].

title: School trainers
text: A radio advert for school trainers is told through messages left by a girl and her grandfather. She is late for [[rehearsal]], he has repaired the [[strap]] of her school bag, and both are trying to find each other outside the hall. The final scene is a rush of footsteps followed by music starting on time. A narrator identifies the trainers, available sizes, price and repair [[guarantee]]. The grandfather's practical help matters, but the girl's performance remains the centre of the story. Her shoes are useful [[equipment]] rather than a magical source of confidence.

title: Designer trainers
text: Before a cinema screening, a designer-trainer advert follows a young dancer arriving at a formal [[audition]]. She changes from polished shoes into brightly coloured trainers just before entering, then performs a piece that mixes street dance with classical steps. The judges' reactions are [[withheld]]; the film ends as she takes a breath after finishing. “Own the terms” appears over a close-up of the shoes, followed by the brand and no price. Her artistic choice drives the [[narrative]], while the campaign converts a challenge to [[institutional]] expectations into an attractive sign of individual style.

title: Waterproof coat
text: A sponsored social post for a waterproof coat is filmed during a weekend search for missing dogs after a storm. A volunteer organiser assigns [[routes]], and a teenager with the advertised coat reports that she has found one animal sheltering near a bridge. The video ends with the dog safely [[reunited]] with its owner. A caption lists the coat's rating, price and the local rescue group's name. The organiser's planning and the teenager's calm [[judgement]] share the credit; the brand's prominent tag nevertheless attaches its product to a community effort carried out by [[volunteers]].

title: Designer coat
text: In a magazine advert for a designer coat, a woman in her seventies stands in a workshop beside a half-finished violin. She has spent decades making instruments, according to a short caption, and a young [[apprentice]] is visible asking her a question. The coat's severe [[silhouette]] echoes the curves of the violin; “Made to be handed on” appears below. There is no price, although the collection name and boutique locations are printed discreetly. The campaign represents older women as makers with authority, while its language of [[inheritance]] also invites the reader to regard an expensive [[garment]] as a lasting possession.

title: Basic handbag
text: A podcast advert for a basic handbag takes the form of a sound diary recorded by a teacher on her journey to work. Keys, train tickets and a [[bundle]] of student drawings emerge from the bag as she describes a class exhibition she has organised. Her colleague phones to say that the display is ready, and the teacher laughs with [[relief]]. The narrator gives the bag's price, measurements and washable [[lining]]. The practical details fit her work, although the cheerful diary [[compresses]] a demanding profession into a handful of charming objects and a successful morning.

title: Designer handbag
text: A website banner for a designer handbag shows a woman translating at an international conference. The screen alternates between her focused expression, a notebook tucked into the bag and the speaker [[whose]] words she is [[conveying]]. “Carry the conversation” leads to product images, materials and an appointment link; the high price appears only after another click. Her expertise is visible and central, yet the banner's visual rhythm repeatedly converts the tools of her profession into [[accessories]]. A small caption identifies the translator by name, giving her a [[specificity]] rarely granted to anonymous luxury models.

title: Everyday fragrance
text: An online video for everyday fragrance follows a young man preparing to meet his partner's parents. He rehearses introductions, forgets a present, and finally arrives carrying a cake bought on the way. His partner opens the door, sees his nervous expression and [[reassures]] him. The fragrance is applied in an early [[mirror]] shot; it does not cause the welcome he receives. “Be there as yourself” appears beside the bottle and a supermarket price. The advert presents [[masculinity]] as capable of [[uncertainty]] and tenderness, although the product still borrows emotional meaning from a relationship it has little power to create.

title: Luxury perfume
text: A billboard for luxury perfume shows a woman at the entrance to an opera house after the audience has left. Her coat is folded over one arm; a programme covered in handwritten notes identifies her as a [[critic]] rather than a performer. “The evening continues in your mind” sits beneath the perfume name in pale [[lettering]]. The bottle is small, and no price interrupts the dark photograph. Her [[intellectual]] response to the performance gives her a role beyond being admired, while the glamorous building and carefully controlled solitude present cultural authority as a form of [[exclusivity]].

title: Budget smartphone
text: A website banner for a budget smartphone features a delivery worker speaking to his mother during a break. When visitors swipe, his mother becomes the central image: she is at a community meeting, using the same phone to show a [[proposal]] for a safer crossing. The next panel lists the handset's battery life, accessibility features and [[upfront]] price. “Make the call. Make the case” ties communication to [[civic]] action. The mother is more than an anxious relative waiting for contact, although the advert's brief format cannot explain [[whether]] the proposed change will actually happen.

title: Flagship smartphone
text: A cinema advert for a flagship smartphone follows a visually impaired musician recording sounds across her city. She identifies a familiar [[pedestrian]] signal, the rattle of a market stall and a friend's footsteps before revealing the short [[composition]] she has made from them. A [[tactile]] phone case and accessibility controls appear alongside the camera and audio features. “Every detail has a story” closes the film, followed by the premium price. Her hearing and creative decisions shape the narrative; the device assists her work without being [[portrayed]] as the reason she can make art.

title: Language-learning app
text: A billboard for a language-learning app shows a restaurant table in two moments. In the first, a traveller reads the menu quietly while the waiter waits; in the second, they discuss a dish, with a speech bubble containing a short, imperfect sentence. “A conversation starts before you are [[fluent]]” appears beside a QR code and the trial terms. The traveller's uncertainty is ordinary rather than comic, and the waiter has an expression of interest rather than [[exaggerated]] amazement. The advert promises a modest social change, although its single [[exchange]] [[necessarily]] simplifies the slower work of learning another language.

title: Gaming headphones
text: A website banner for gaming headphones depicts an esports team discussing a failed match. The [[captain]] listens while a quieter member explains the mistake everyone missed; moving captions reproduce each player's words, and an audio button demonstrates the headset's microphone. “Hear the whole team” links to specifications, [[compatibility]] information and the price. The team's authority is [[distributed]] across different voices, including a girl whose suggestion changes the plan. Their cooperative scene is carefully selected to make a [[commercial]] feature feel like a lesson in respect and communication. The team's final result remains unseen.

title: Premium noise-cancelling headphones
text: This television advert for premium noise-cancelling headphones follows a father taking the train to visit his adult daughter. He puts on the headphones to hear an old recording of her practising violin as a child, then removes them when she boards at the next station and sits beside him. The music continues softly under their conversation. A final card explains [[adjustable]] listening modes and gives the high price. The story treats quiet as a choice, not an [[escape]] from other people, though its emotional [[weight]] comes from a relationship [[established]] long before the product enters the scene.

title: Family tablet
text: A radio advert for a family tablet begins with a grandmother reading a story to children who live in another city. One child keeps [[interrupting]] to correct her description of the dragon; later, they show her a drawing on the tablet's shared screen. The narrator explains the video-call controls and a family price, with a note about parental settings. Their [[affection]] is conveyed through disagreement and laughter rather than a [[sentimental]] speech. The grandmother is the storyteller, while the children supply the pictures, allowing each generation to [[contribute]] something the other could not have prepared alone.

title: Professional camera
text: An online video for a professional camera follows a local journalist covering a flood. She photographs residents organising supplies, checks a caption with one volunteer and chooses not to publish an image of a [[distressed]] child. The camera's weather [[sealing]] and low-light performance are demonstrated without interrupting her decisions. A final link provides [[specifications]] and the premium price. The campaign presents responsible image-making as part of professional skill, although the flood also supplies a dramatic setting for selling equipment. Names and locations in the finished photographs are shown only where [[permission]] has been granted.

title: Fitness tracker
text: This transit poster for a fitness tracker places an older woman between two versions of the same walk. On the left she rests at a bench; on the right, weeks later, she reaches a garden she has wanted to visit. The headline says, “Your route can change.” A smaller panel shows the tracker, price and options for adjusting activity goals. Her progress is personal and [[uncompetitive]], but the poster's neat before-and-after structure suggests a steadier path than most [[recovery]] allows. A note under the image [[identifies]] the woman as a community [[gardener]] and names the public garden.

title: Home security system
text: A television advert for a home security system begins when a boy notices that his elderly neighbour's lights have remained off. His father checks the camera at their shared entrance, then walks over and learns that she has simply gone away for the weekend. She later returns with a joke about being watched. The final card explains [[consent]] settings, alert sharing and the monthly fee. The story grants the neighbour [[independence]] and a voice, while the family's initial concern makes [[surveillance]] appear reassuring. Her joke leaves the question of who decides what should be [[monitored]] open rather than fully settled.

title: Entry-level laptop
text: In a radio advert for an entry-level laptop, a woman describes her first evening class after years away from education. We hear the keyboard, her tutor's patient explanation and the surprised laugh that follows when her presentation finally works. A second voice explains the price, battery life and low-cost repairs. “Begin with the work in front of you” closes the segment. Her uncertainty is [[temporary]] but real, and the tutor is present without taking over. The [[compressed]] narrative ends in success, yet it gives the learner, rather than the machine, [[credit]] for the effort [[required]].

title: Family car
text: A magazine advert for a family car shows a teenager loading equipment for her wheelchair basketball team into the boot. Her younger brother holds the door while their mother checks the [[accessible]] route to the sports centre. The photograph places the athlete at its centre, with the vehicle's seating and [[storage]] details in a side panel. “The game starts before the [[whistle]]” connects transport to [[participation]]. A clearly printed price and safety information follow. The family members are helping her reach a match she has chosen; their care does not replace her ambition or make her disability the campaign's only subject.

title: Luxury car
text: An online video for a luxury car follows a chef driving home after closing her restaurant. She stops at a late-night market, speaks with a [[supplier]] and chooses ingredients for tomorrow's menu. The car's quiet interior contrasts with the lively street, while the camera lingers on her hands checking produce rather than merely holding the [[steering]] wheel. “For those who decide what comes next” appears beside the brand, without a price. Her expertise and ownership of the journey are clear. The market workers, however, supply texture and [[authenticity]] without receiving the same [[narrative]] attention.

title: City bicycle
text: A billboard for a city bicycle shows a teenage girl teaching her father the safest route to a new community centre. Their bikes are stopped at a crossing while she points towards a [[protected]] lane. “Know your way around” sits above the brand, price and a QR code for local route maps. The [[reversal]] of familiar parent-child [[instruction]] gives the girl useful knowledge, and the visible crossing keeps the city from becoming an unreal traffic-free playground. Still, the advert depends on safe cycling [[infrastructure]] that the bicycle itself cannot provide.

title: Racing bicycle
text: On a billboard for a racing bicycle, the rider is shown after rather than during a race. She leans against a wall, exhausted, while her coach examines the bike's [[chain]] and a teammate brings water. The line “Built for the work between finishes” appears beside the frame's weight and the brand name. The high price is accessible through a QR code, not printed on the main image. Her [[fatigue]] and the supporting team complicate the [[solitary]] champion image, although the brand remains positioned as an essential part of their [[collective]] achievement.

title: Budget hotel stay
text: A television advert for a budget hotel stay follows two friends visiting a coastal town in winter. Their small room overlooks a car park, but the receptionist gives them directions to a quieter beach, and they return with [[windblown]] hair and takeaway supper. The final card gives the actual room [[rate]], booking conditions and walking time to the station. “Spend the day somewhere new” is the only slogan. By allowing the view to disappoint, the advert makes its low price [[credible]]; the receptionist also gets a name and knowledge of the place rather than appearing as [[anonymous]] service.

title: Luxury hotel stay
text: A transit poster for a luxury hotel shows a guest looking out across a city from an [[immaculate]] room. In the mirror behind her, a housekeeper adjusts the curtains; the reflection is sharp enough to show her expression, but she is unnamed. “A view made for you” appears above a [[discreet]] booking code and the suite's name. The absence of a price and the elevated viewpoint construct a [[privileged]] audience. The composition makes the worker [[literally]] visible within the luxury being sold, while still placing her at the edge of the guest's experience.

title: Household vacuum cleaner
text: A billboard for a household vacuum cleaner depicts a crowded [[multigenerational]] home after a family celebration. A grandfather vacuums fallen paper decorations while two children collect plates and their aunt carries chairs away. “Everyone can finish the party” appears beside the product, a large price and its warranty. The mess is specific and believable, and no one person is given permanent [[responsibility]] for cleaning it. Yet the [[celebratory]] context softens the routine nature of housework, making the machine seem [[associated]] with happy occasions rather than the tasks repeated every day.

title: Premium robot vacuum
text: In a magazine advert for a premium robot vacuum, a [[composer]] works at a piano while the device travels through her apartment. A second image shows her partner emptying its container and moving a cable out of the way. “More time for the unfinished piece” appears beside the model's name; the price and [[maintenance]] requirements sit in a clear panel. The campaign acknowledges that [[automation]] needs human attention, although the composer receives the [[aspirational]] close-up. Their apartment's broad, uncluttered floor also makes the device's performance look easier than it might in a smaller home.

title: Flat-pack sofa
text: An online video for a flat-pack sofa follows three friends moving into a shared apartment. One reads the instructions, another sorts the parts and the third keeps turning a panel the wrong way; the edit [[retains]] their laughter and an argument about which colour cushion to use. A time-lapse then gives way to a quiet final scene in which they sit down together. The price, delivery charge and [[assembly]] guide appear on screen. “Make somewhere to stay” links furniture to a [[tentative]] sense of home, without [[disguising]] the work of putting it together.

title: Designer sofa
text: A podcast advert for a designer sofa invites listeners into a conversation between an [[upholsterer]] and a customer whose daughter uses a wheelchair. They discuss seat depth, fabric that can be cleaned easily and how everyone will gather in the room. The daughter joins the recording and rejects an impractical arrangement the adults had agreed on. The host offers a design appointment and names the collection, but gives no price. Her [[intervention]] makes her a user with [[preferences]] rather than an abstract accessibility problem; the bespoke service [[simultaneously]] assumes the family can pay for substantial choice.

title: Shampoo
text: A transit poster for shampoo features a teenage boy with long hair, tying it back before a school science demonstration. A classmate holds the equipment while he checks his notes. “Ready for whatever you are making” is printed beside the bottle, price and a simple claim about gentle washing. The image broadens who can be seen in hair-care advertising without making his appearance a [[spectacle]]. The laboratory setting supplies an identity beyond [[grooming]], even though a glossy [[strand]] of hair remains carefully lit across the centre of the poster. His [[experiment]], rather than his hair, attracts the class's attention.

title: Premium skincare serum
text: A television advert for premium skincare serum follows an older woman leading a coastal clean-up. She explains how [[tides]] carry plastic into a sheltered bay, then returns home and applies the serum after washing her face. The bottle is shown clearly only in the final seconds, when a caption lists its ingredients, price and the [[scope]] of its claims. Her [[expertise]] and physical work structure the story; her age remains visible. The campaign borrows moral weight from [[environmental]] action, however, without claiming that the expensive product itself addresses the problem she describes.

title: Mobile data plan
text: A transit poster for a mobile data plan shows a young man translating a voice message for his father at a bus stop. Beside them, the father's reply is printed in two languages: he has already understood the important part. “Keep every conversation open” leads to the allowance, monthly price and [[roaming]] limits. The father is [[neither]] helpless nor silent; the exchange shows [[cooperation]] across languages and generations. Its neat two-line conversation nevertheless reduces the [[complexity]] of maintaining family ties across countries to a service that can be purchased by the month.

title: Private tutoring service
text: In a podcast advert for private tutoring, a student reads a paragraph from her history essay and stops when she realises her [[evidence]] does not support the point. Her tutor asks what she actually wants to argue; we hear her revise the sentence aloud. The host then gives qualifications, session length and a high hourly fee. “Find the words for your own thinking” closes the segment. The student retains [[authorship]], and the tutoring is presented as [[questioning]] rather than answer-giving. The price makes clear that this kind of individual attention remains [[unevenly]] available.

title: Gym membership
text: A transit poster for a gym membership shows the same class at three moments: entering uncertainly, resting between exercises and leaving in conversation. A man with a larger body is central in the middle photograph, but no image asks viewers to compare his shape before and after. “A place to return to” appears beside the monthly price, accessibility details and opening hours. The [[sequencing]] values belonging and [[persistence]] over visible transformation. Its cheerful group, however, cannot represent everyone who might feel uncomfortable crossing the [[threshold]] for the first time. A trial session is offered without promising that [[discomfort]] will vanish.

title: Wellness retreat
text: A sponsored social post for a wellness retreat is narrated by a woman who says she came because she needed time to make a difficult decision. We see her walking, writing a letter and speaking briefly with a counsellor, but the decision itself remains private. The caption lists the retreat's activities, [[credentials]], dates and substantial cost. “Leave with a little more room” promises no instant cure. Her refusal to [[disclose]] the [[outcome]] gives her control over the story, although the campaign still turns a private period of [[uncertainty]] into an appealing destination.

title: Children’s board game
text: A website banner for a children's board game shows a brother and sister arguing about the rules while their aunt waits for them to settle it. When the [[cursor]] moves, the banner reveals each child's [[proposed]] solution and the game's actual rule. “Someone always sees another move” links to the age range, playing time and price. Their disagreement is an [[intellectual]] part of the play, not a problem solved by an adult. The interactive format invites viewers to choose a side, giving the children [[distinct]] arguments rather than using their smiles as proof of family happiness.

title: Collectable toy set
text: A radio advert for a collectable toy set takes the form of an interview with a child who has invented a story for the figures. She describes a scientist, a pilot and a [[mechanic]] escaping a [[collapsing]] city, but insists that the mechanic should decide where they go. Sound effects briefly bring her plot to life. A narrator names the figures and gives each separate price. The child's imaginative [[authority]] makes the toys seem open-ended, while the [[elaborate]] adventure encourages listeners to picture a complete set rather than one affordable purchase.

title: Streaming subscription
text: This television advert for a streaming subscription follows an older woman choosing a documentary about a place where she once lived. Her grandson assumes she wants a [[nostalgic]] programme, but she pauses to challenge the film's account of a local [[protest]] she [[remembers]] differently. The screen then shows them searching for another source together. “A story can start a conversation” appears with the subscription price and trial terms. Her memory becomes knowledge rather than a sentimental reaction, although the platform still positions its [[catalogue]] as the convenient starting point for that exchange.

title: Premium bank account
text: A magazine advert for a premium bank account depicts a woman reviewing documents in a railway lounge while her teenage son reads beside her. A caption identifies her as the [[founder]] of a small export business, and the benefits panel lists international payments, travel support, [[eligibility]] rules and the monthly fee. “Work crosses borders. So can your plans” appears in restrained type. Her professional choices are specific, yet the comfortable lounge and [[seamless]] journey compress the difficulties of running a business across countries into an image of [[composure]] available through financial privilege.
